title: tozero Delivers Recycled Lithium Carbonate to German Industrial Customer - Batteries News

tozero Delivers Recycled Lithium Carbonate to German Industrial Customer
Burgkirchen / Munich, Germany, November 5, 2026
— tozero, a German deep-tech company recovering critical raw materials from lithium-ion battery waste, has completed its first delivery of recycled lithium carbonate produced at its demonstration plant at Chemical Park Gendorf to a German ceramics customer.
The delivery demonstrates tozero’s ability to recover lithium from battery waste and produce recycled lithium carbonate tailored to the requirements of an industrial customer.
The shipment represents an important milestone toward execution of the companies’ long-term binding offtake agreement and future recurring supply.
“Delivering a product that meets the requirements of an industrial customer is an important moment for any deep-tech company. It reflects years of dedication, problem-solving and determination by our team. From the beginning, we believed that innovation needs to have a clear industrial purpose and that every euro invested should move us closer to creating real value for our customers,” said Dr. Ksenija Neumann, founder and Co-CEO of tozero.
The lithium carbonate was produced at tozero’s demonstration plant at Chemical Park Gendorf, where the company is validating its recycling technology, product quality and process performance under customer-relevant conditions.
Since launching operations in Gendorf, tozero has focused on increasing operational stability, validating its process at larger scale and producing materials for customer qualification.
Building new industrial technology requires creativity, discipline and a willingness to challenge conventional thinking,
“We have been deliberate in how we deploy capital: first prove the technology, then validate it with customers, and use those learnings to design the next stage of industrial scale-up. This delivery is another important step along that path.”
Customer Validation
— Daniel Schulze Zur Verth,
Managing Director of Botz GmbH, said:
Receiving recycled lithium carbonate from tozero marks an important milestone in our collaboration and reflects our shared ambition to build more sustainable, resilient and regionally anchored supply chains.
“Increasing the use of recycled raw materials will be an important part of reducing reliance on primary resources and lowering the environmental footprint of industrial production. We are pleased to take this step together with tozero and look forward to expanding the role of circular materials in our future production.”
Serving Multiple Industries with Recycled Lithium
tozero’s recycled lithium can address the needs of multiple industries facing increasing pressure on raw-material supply.
Beyond batteries, sectors such as ceramics also depend on reliable access to lithium and are looking for more sustainable alternatives to primary raw materials.
For tozero, this is an important part of the vision: enabling different industries to access regionally sourced, recycled critical materials while reducing dependence on primary extraction and imported supply.
At the same time, tozero continues advancing the technology toward additional applications, including battery-grade lithium materials.
The ability to recover lithium from end-of-life batteries and manufacture products according to different customer specifications is an important part of tozero’s strategy.
Rather than attempting to control every stage of the battery recycling value chain, the company focuses on the recovery and refining of valuable critical raw materials from black mass.
This approach reduces capital intensity while enabling tozero to work with existing collection, preprocessing and industrial supply-chain partners.
Automotive Industry Perspective
While tozero sees significant potential to serve multiple industries that depend on lithium, the company continues to advance its technology toward battery-grade applications and the long-term objective of returning recycled lithium from end-of-life batteries back into battery production.
— Axel Strotbek,
former automotive executive and business angel, said:
This is exactly the kind of industrial progress we want to see.
”Demonstrating the ability to recover lithium from used batteries and produce recycled lithium carbonate to a customer’s specification is an important step toward the ultimate goal of battery-grade materials. Less than 2% of the available black mass is processed to extract lithium in Europe. That is why building a resilient European battery value chain requires more than promising technology — it requires demonstrated execution, strong industrial partnerships and a clear pathway toward scale.”
Strengthening European Critical Raw Material Supply
Europe remains highly dependent on imported critical raw materials used across batteries and other strategic industries.
Recovering materials such as lithium from existing battery waste provides an opportunity to retain valuable resources within regional supply chains while reducing dependency on primary raw-material extraction and imports.
Preparing for the Next Stage of Industrial Scale-Up
Following the progress achieved at its Gendorf demonstration plant and the start of customer product deliveries, tozero is preparing for its next phase of industrial scale-up.
The next phase will build on the technical validation, operating experience and customer relationships established through the Gendorf demonstration plant.
Our objective is not simply to prove that lithium can be recovered from battery waste,
“We want to build a scalable industrial business around it. Customer validation is what connects technology with the market, and this delivery brings us another step closer to that goal.”

title: European Industrial Sovereignty: Veolia Launches a Pioneering Site for Extracting Strategic Metals From EV Batteries - Batteries News
content:
European Industrial Sovereignty: Veolia Launches a Pioneering Site for Extracting Strategic Metals From EV Batteries
The key link in the value chain to
strengthen geostrategic autonomy in Europe
A concrete commitment to building a sovereign and circular European value chain
, ensuring a local supply for European automotive, construction and defense industries and, in the long term, with the support of public authorities, the manufacturing of batteries in Europe (“battery to battery”)
A cutting-edge technology enables the recovery of more than 90% of the cobalt, nickel, and copper contained in the black mass
resulting from battery shredding
A major potential market: nearly
700,000 tonnes of batteries to be processed within five years
in Europe, representing an estimated value of more than
one billion euros in strategic metals
BUSINESS WIRE
)–Regulatory News:
Veolia (Paris:VIE) is paving the way with a groundbreaking project to reclaim European sovereignty over strategic metals.
The group is launching a pioneering initiative in the Grand Est region (France), in the presence of Estelle Brachlianoff, CEO of Veolia, Stéphane Séjourné, Executive Vice-President of the European Commission in charge of prosperity and industrial strategy, and Franck Leroy, President of the Grand Est Region.
Recovering strategic metals such as nickel and cobalt is a major issue of competitiveness and sovereignty for Europe, aiming to reduce its dependence on imports and to stop its valuable resources from being shipped abroad. Today, extra-European competition is driving a massive export of black mass to Asia. Yet
within five years, nearly 700,000 tonnes of batteries are expected to be recycled in Europe, representing more than one billion euros’ worth of recoverable metals.
Guided by this vision, Veolia has brought to life this first European project equipped with proprietary hydrometallurgy technologies to process black mass flows from Europe (from France, the United Kingdom and Switzerland to date). The innovative process makes it possible to dismantle batteries, efficiently separate the black mass and, ultimately, extract cobalt, nickel and copper from it. These metals are then redistributed to the European automotive, construction and defense markets.
Each year, the site will be able to recycle nearly 7,000 tonnes of black mass, the equivalent of 20,000 tonnes of batteries.
Pioneering in this field, Veolia is steadfastly pursuing its efforts to build a European battery recycling value chain. Several projects dedicated to battery dismantling, complementary to the processing activities of this state-of-the-art facility located downstream in the value chain, are currently being deployed in the United Kingdom, Belgium and Slovenia.
Europe’s backing is vital to securing a domestic supply of strategic metals. It is also essential for building a circular industrial model, by supporting the establishment of facilities that can reintegrate recycled metals. This calls for a Europe-wide regulatory and economic framework to be put in place now.
Estelle Brachlianoff
, CEO of Veolia, said:
Through its technologies and pioneering expertise, Veolia is helping to create a sovereign supply of strategic metals from recycling.
”Thanks to this facility, where European black mass flows converge, this extraordinary resource can be recovered within Europe: today serving the metallurgy sector and, tomorrow perhaps, producing new European batteries. This is the very purpose of our commitments and of the ambitions carried by our Green Up strategic programme: turning waste into a strategic resource and circular industry into a competitiveness lever serving local regions. The challenge is a collective one, on a key issue for our industry and our economy,”
Stéphane Séjourné,
Executive Vice President of the European Commission, said:
For too long, Europe has watched its strategic raw materials leave the continent, only to import finished products from elsewhere. We must break free from this cycle of dependency.
”This new plant in the Grand Est region is ‘Made in Europe’ in action: resources recycled in Europe, processed in Europe, to power our batteries in Europe. This is the very essence of the industrial shift we are championing: safeguarding our resources, supporting our manufacturers, and turning European preference into reality. Through the Battery Regulation, the Industrial Accelerator Act, and the upcoming Circular Economy Act, we are equipping ourselves with the tools to achieve this ambition. The green transition must also be a policy of industrial sovereignty, production, and employment in Europe,”
Franck Leroy,
President of the Grand Est Region, said:
The installation of this state-of-the-art recycling facility is a strong sign of our region’s economic vitality and capacity for innovation.
”The Grand Est Region is extremely proud to have supported this pioneering project from day one: a true industrial showcase on both the national and European levels. We owe this success to the joint efforts of all local stakeholders. It proves that by combining our strengths and expertise, we are capable of building together a circular economy that creates value for our area, our economy, and, above all, European energy sovereignty,”

title: LG Energy Solution Vertech Launches AEROS™ Intelligence to Turn Battery Data into Actionable Insights - Batteries News
content:
LG Energy Solution Vertech Launches AEROS™ Intelligence to Turn Battery Data into Actionable Insights
AEROS™ Intelligence offers up to 90% reduction in downtime for some corrective maintenance actions
AEROS™ Intelligence reduces state of charge error by about 30%-50%
The new offering is built on operating data from more than 17 years of energy storage management and supports a unified AEROS™ software suite from LG Energy Solution Vertech for smarter energy storage projects
WESTBOROUGH, Mass., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — LG Energy Solution Vertech has launched AEROS™ Intelligence, a new platform that transforms energy storage system data into actionable insights, helping asset owners, operators, and energy market participants improve performance, reduce downtime, and maximize long-term returns from their energy storage investments.
As battery energy storage systems play an increasingly critical role in power markets, operators face growing challenges in managing asset health, maintaining performance, predicting maintenance needs, and balancing revenue generation with long-term battery value. AEROS™ Intelligence enables customers to transform raw site information and battery data into clear opportunities for more informed decision making throughout project lifecycles. Through site-specific degradation insights and warranty-aware operating guidance, AEROS™ Intelligence can help customers defer battery augmentation for around 1.5 years and preserve millions in capital value over the life of the project.
AEROS™ Intelligence serves as the analytics layer underpinning the broader AEROS™ software suite, which includes AEROS™ Onsite for real-time energy management and plant controls, and AEROS™ Cloud for monitoring and reporting. Together, the suite provides integrated controls, optimization tools, and advanced monitoring capabilities designed to optimize site functionality and maximize return on investment.
Built as a unified decision-support platform, AEROS™ Intelligence delivers four key capabilities designed to help storage owners operate more efficiently and proactively.
BESS Health
: Gain early, actionable insights into battery degradation and site health. Leveraging BESS Health and Warranty Hub together can help customers defer battery augmentation for around 1.5 years and preserve millions in capital value over the life of the project
Predictive Maintenance
: Identify and address risks early to prevent outages and reduce downtime. Predictive Maintenance offers up to 90% reduction in downtime for some corrective maintenance actions
Energy Optimizer
: Turn battery insight into smarter dispatch and revenue uplift through intelligence that balances asset life and revenue opportunity. Energy Optimizer reduces state of charge error by about 30%-50%
Warranty Hub
: Monitor critical KPIs, track warranties, assess the current status of assets based on contract terms, and monitor remaining headroom
Tristan Doherty,
Chief Product Officer at LG Energy Solution Vertech, said:
Battery energy storage has become a critical infrastructure asset for the modern grid, but managing these systems efficiently goes beyond system technology,
“We’re working to provide a comprehensive ecosystem that knits together complex storage systems, lifecycle services, and an advanced software suite – to give customers the most accurate view possible into their operational efficiency and ROI. AEROS™ Intelligence represents the next evolution of energy storage software, providing customers with the data, intelligence, and actionable insights they need to maximize asset value and support a more resilient energy future.”
As energy storage deployments continue to grow in size and complexity, and project fleets expand across the country, operators are left with a growing need for a frictionless vertically integrated solution provider with advanced software that maps out an energy storage approach that works for their unique circumstances.
AEROS™ Intelligence supports this need by combining LG Energy Solution battery design data with more than 17 years of operating fleet data from LG Energy Solution Vertech. AEROS™ Intelligence uses advanced analytics and insights to help customers move from reactive asset management to proactive decision making.

title: FIXX Energy Celebrates 5 Million American-Made LFP Battery Cells - Batteries News
content:
FIXX Energy Celebrates 5 Million American-Made LFP Battery Cells
Smyrna, Tennessee facility reaches a new production milestone as demand for domestic energy storage accelerates
SMYRNA, Tenn., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — FIXX Energy, the first American-owned and operated manufacturer of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells for grid-scale energy storage systems (ESS), has produced more than five million cells at its Smyrna facility since converting the plant to LFP cell production in April 2025. Combined, the cells represent roughly 5 GWh of energy storage capacity, enough to carry 1 million U.S. homes through an evening peak. Laid end to end, they would stretch from FIXX’s Tennessee plant to Washington, D.C.
FIXX’s cells are deployed in battery energy storage projects nationwide, strengthening the electric grid and making energy more reliable and affordable for American homes and businesses. FIXX Energy and its cells help integrators and end users qualify for Section 45X Advanced Manufacturing Production Tax Credits and Section 48E Investment Tax Credits, including the domestic content bonus, under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Jeff Juger,
CEO of FIXX Energy, said:
Five million cells is five million proof points that America can build the energy storage foundation our grid needs, right here at home,
“Our team in Smyrna has demonstrated what American manufacturing can accomplish. Every cell we’ve produced has taught us something, and we’re finding new ways to put that experience to work, including using artificial intelligence to drive further improvements in quality, efficiency, and cost. As demand for energy storage continues to grow, we’re proud to be delivering the reliable, American-made battery cells our customers need.”
The milestone also reflects the Town of Smyrna’s long-standing support for the facility, which began operations in 2012.
Mary Esther Reed,
Mayor of Smyrna, said:
Smyrna has a proud legacy of advanced manufacturing, and reaching five million cells produced is a tremendous achievement for both FIXX Energy and our community,
“This milestone is a direct testament to the dedication and skill of our local workforce. We are proud that these battery cells are being built right here in Smyrna.”
FIXX is proud to contribute to America’s growing energy storage manufacturing base. According to the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, domestic battery module and system manufacturing capacity now exceeds total U.S. project demand, but battery cell production still lags, leaving a critical gap in a fully domestic supply chain. FIXX is helping close that gap, and its Smyrna facility is part of the energy storage industry’s $100 billion commitment to build American factories and buy American-made batteries, an investment expected to create more than 350,000 American jobs by the end of the decade.
Noah Roberts,
Executive Director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, said:
Energy storage has proven essential for ensuring regional power grid reliability and lowering electricity prices.
”As we race to keep up with surging demand for electricity and energy storage resources, our continued success depends on the strength of our U.S. supply chains and investment in American factorie. FIXX’s milestone shows what that investment means for American communities: more manufacturing jobs and greater energy security.”

title: QuantumScape Expands Commercial Roadmap with Osprey, the Open All-Solid-State Platform for Battery Development - Batteries News
content:
QuantumScape Expands Commercial Roadmap with Osprey, the Open All-Solid-State Platform for Battery Development
SAN JOSE, Calif. — November 11, 2026 —
QuantumScape Corporation
(NASDAQ: QS), a global leader in solid-state lithium-metal battery technology, today announced Osprey: its next-generation open platform for all-solid-state batteries. Osprey cells have delivered the world’s first public data demonstrating a sulfide-based cathode cycling 1,000 times under just one atmosphere of pressure – an unmatched capability that is necessary for automotive solid-state batteries.
Osprey pairs the QS proprietary ceramic separator and anode-free lithium-metal design with a solid cathode, creating an all-solid-state cell. Osprey builds on the company’s QSE platform, and opens new licensing and co-development options for current QS customers and expanding its offering to developers of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries.
QS technology has demonstrated an enhanced safety profile compared to conventional lithium-ion cells, along with low operating pressure and excellent energy retention. Osprey’s all-solid cathode, paired with the proprietary QS ceramic separator, enables additional performance benefits, including faster charging, operation across a wider range of temperatures, and projected energy densities up to ~1,100 Wh/L.
In early testing, Osprey cells have demonstrated:
Cycle life:
1,000 full charge cycles with ~80% capacity retention under gold-standard testing conditions
Fast charging:
10% to 80% in five-minutes
Low pressure:
Requires only one atmosphere of pressure
Cold-weather performance:
Operational to less than -20 °C (-4 °F)
More information, including test results and conditions, can be found in a
new white paper.
The battery industry has long pursued all-solid-state batteries using sulfide-based electrolytes, but this has yet to result in a commercially viable technology. Sulfides can react with lithium metal, which shortens battery life, and they typically need to be held under high pressure to operate, which is impractical for vehicles and many other applications.
Osprey is conceived as an open platform capable of working with a range of cathode chemistries. QS has tested Osprey with all-solid cathodes developed both in-house and by its automotive customers, laying the groundwork for multiple technology pathways for solid-state battery development.
Dr. Siva Sivaram,
president and CEO of QS, said:
Osprey is the result of years of frontier R&D efforts, and we’re excited to share it publicly for the first time,
“The industry has invested heavily in sulfide-based batteries but keeps hitting the same fundamental limits. As the data shows, Osprey can address these limitations. We believe Osprey can unlock the full potential of all-solid-state batteries, and our goal is to make it the leading platform for solid-state battery development.”
QS is already working with partners across the automotive industry on development using the Osprey platform. Cells based on the company’s QSE platform are shipping to customers today, and Osprey represents its long-term technology solution for all-solid-state battery development.

title: How Peak Energy Chose Sodium-Ion for Grid Storage
content:
Stationary Batteries
Materials
Battery Manufacturing
Interviews
Peak Energy develops sodium-ion battery storage for the grid, focused on safety, lower costs, and US manufacturing for large-scale energy deployment.
November 13, 2026
7 Min Read
Peak Energy has garnered more than $1 billion in commercial customer agreements.
Peak Energy.
Cameron Dales was certain that he was done with launching and managing startup organizations. It was 2023, and his career to that point was almost completely dedicated to introducing the high-tech hub that is California’s Silicon Valley to new companies. As a member of the founding teams for Symyx Technologies, a former materials science group that developed high-throughput robotic tools and software for the discovery and processing of advanced materials before being acquisitioned, and the advanced lithium-ion battery outfit
, where he led commercial strategy and operations, Dales had no doubts — the time was right for a new direction.
When an opportunity to join Eclipse Ventures in Palo Alto, a firm that he had brought to Enovix as its largest investor, was presented to serve as an operating partner, he accepted. “I really thought my days of company-building were over,” said Dales, president and chief commercial officer at Peak Energy, a startup that produces a battery energy storage system (BESS) based on sodium-ion technology. And he continued to feel that way up to and including the first day of his new job, when a chance meeting with former Tesla executive Landon Mossburg.
Related:
This Tech Issue Is Reshaping the 2026 Midterm Elections
“I remember distinctly telling Landon that nothing could ever beat lithium-ion,” Dales recalls. “That you couldn’t make money in grid storage and, by the way, that I would never be interested in starting another company. But I did wish him good luck.” Within a few months’ time, however, Dales came to the conclusion that lithium-ion was not going to be the best long-standing platform for an anticipated multi-decade infrastructure uprising in the grid storage sector.
ESS Gigafactory Sacramento. Courtesy of Peak Energy.
Why Peak Energy chose sodium-ion for grid-scale energy storage
Demand for longer storage durations at lower costs was only going to escalate, even before factoring in the expansion of renewable energy and data centers. “The most exciting opportunity in all of energy was going to be this massive build-out that is happening,” said Dales. “A trillion dollars would be going into the ground over the next 10 years, and it would be the linchpin to speed-to-electrons for data centers. It would be the key to low-cost electricity given the growing demand across the economy. It’s an incredibly exciting market. And we realized that we could develop at a scale that had never been seen before in stationary batteries that were being built on the wrong technology platform.”
Today, Peak Energy, has garnered more than $1 billion in commercial customer agreements and has recently announced $108 million through its most recent round of financing capital to begin installations of the company’s proprietary
passively cooled
sodium-ion BESS, which is said to be the first of its kind in the United States.
Related:
How Gotion Built Its 40-GWh Gigafactory in Illinois
How Peak Energy’s sodium-ion BESS improves safety and lowers OPEX
Dales built a career advancing battery and aerospace technologies. With engineering degrees from Cornell and Stanford, he developed spacecraft hardware at Lockheed Martin, co-founded Symyx Technologies’ Tools unit, and led automated research tool development. At Enovix, he helped establish infrastructure, technology, and partnerships for manufacturing ultra-high-performance 3D silicon-wafer batteries successfully.
He can lay claim to more than 100 patents as an inventor. He says that one of the key takeaways he learned along the pathway that led him to Mossburg and the staff that they’ve cultivated at Peak, which consists of founding members largely from Tesla, Enovix, and
Northvolt,
is that lithium-ion is essentially developed for mobile technology. “It is focused on high-energy density as opposed to the things that really matter in stationary storage, with cost being No. 1 as well as fire safety, and, more importantly, the security of the supply chain,” Dales said.
Related:
Should Batteries Be Beautiful? Torus Thinks So.
Alongside this reality, he saw what he calls the “sister technology” of lithium-ion emerging in China—the class of sodium-ion batteries. “After spending a significant amount of time visiting factories in China, we became convinced that this was really going to reach scale, which is a prerequisite for any chemistry or any technology to actually make any difference in the battery space,” said Dales. “And we believed that it was going to reach scale faster than anybody really was expecting in the Western world. With that, we launched Peak Energy with a vision to not just be a battery company but to attack the most impactful part of the challenge first, which is the storage piece. We’ve recruited an amazing team that could rethink how to design and architect a stationary storage system when you're starting with a different building block.”
Despite some inherent differences, sodium remains quite similar to
lithium iron phosphate (LFP)
in several ways and can be manufactured on the same platform. “With lithium-ion, you can literally switch over an LFP production line to sodium-ion,” explained Dales. “So we had a running start in terms of scale.”
Peak's grid storage product. Courtesy of Peak Energy.
Why passive architecture matters for grid-scale battery safety
“This can be mitigated at the system level, but that comes at the expense of complexity and cost,” said Dales. “You build very complex systems to keep them safe, especially when you've got hundreds of giant container-sized batteries together to form a project. As we started rethinking how energy storage should be done with this different building block, sodium, we found that the main disadvantage of sodium-ion is that it's somewhat lower energy density. That means it's definitely not the right choice for your cell phone.” In the context of stationary storage, however, the density impact was not determined to be significant. “What we found as we started working with it and designing specifically for that chemistry — was that its unique properties were really around stability,” said Dales. “Stability over its lifetime. Stability over cycle life. And stability for safety reasons. It's less volatile and highly stable at high temperatures.”
While lithium-ion batteries have become less expensive and the cost around facilities built with large stationary batteries has decreased, almost all of that reduction has come from the cell and doesn’t solve the real ongoing economic difficulty, which lies with the systems, said Dales. “It's in the installation. It’s in sending an army of electricians to the field to wire systems up over weeks, sometimes months. And the biggest piece of the pie is the operating expense (OPEX) line. The cost to operate what are essentially power plants for decades. And the OPEX line is driven by a host of factors, such as the degradation of batteries over time and the need to then replace them to live up to power purchase agreements, as well as preventive maintenance.”
Since launching the company in 2023, Dales says he and his team have substantially improved the capabilities of sodium-ion at high temperatures. “They now allow us to build a system that is ideal in simplicity,” he said. “Our units have no cooling system and no fire-suppression system required because of the safety properties of the chemistry. It's a fully passive architecture. There’s no moving parts and no coolants to leak, which typically is how fires start. It's not the cell spontaneously combusting, it's the ancillary electronics and coolants. There's no preventive maintenance required for our system.”
Peak Energy’s Sacramento factory, customer pipeline, and GM partnership
This summer, Dales and his colleagues announced that Sacramento, CA, will be home to Peak’s first US manufacturing facility dedicated to grid-scale sodium-ion BESS. The
183,000-square-foot facility
located in Sacramento's Metro Air Park is expected to enter production with shipments beginning in the first quarter of 2027 and will reportedly produce up to 4 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery systems annually, in addition to more than 6 GWh of customer commitments already in place.
Secured customer agreements include those with Jupiter Power, Energy Vault, and RWE Americas. The company also recently announced a
strategic partnership with General Motors
that will reportedly combine Peak's BESS technology with GM's battery cell development expertise to deliver more affordable and reliable stationary storage. “And then there is a robust pipeline of additional projects and longer, larger offtakes that we expect to sign over the course of the rest of this year,” said Dales.

Supply Chain Digital explores the top five stories from the past week, including news from DP World, Walmart and Hyundai
DP World Expands Shipping Network for Operational Resilience
DP World is undergoing a period of expansion, with the launch of the China Africa link.
Around the world, shipping is becoming more complex and more unreliable. As a result, businesses are
forming new trade routes
in order to simplify shipping and add new options for their clients.
The launch of this new route is strengthening maritime connections and offering access to new and expanding markets.
Exiger Secures US Air Force ICBM Supply Chain Risk Contract
Exiger, a market-leading supply chain risk management company, has been awarded a US$12 million contract by the US Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center. The contract focuses on enhancing the Intercontinental Ballistic Missile (ICBM) Systems Directorate by delivering advanced multi-tier supply chain illumination and deep Defence Industrial Base (DIB) analytics.
"Ensuring 24/7 readiness in lockstep alongside strategic modernization is one of the most consequential missions in U.S. national security. This requires both the long-term orchestration of multiple strategic, sensitive supplier bases while very actively mapping and mitigating adversarial threats to the supply chain," says Scott LaFoy, Vice President of Nuclear and Technology Security Programs at Exiger.
"Exiger’s differentiated strength is our ability to connect supplier risk to the parts, materials, facilities, and industrial base dependencies that actually drive mission readiness and program performance."
Jabil is offering supply chain management and procurement consulting with its new portfolio. Credit: Getty
Jabil Develops New Resilient Supply Chain Portfolio
Jabil has consolidated five acquired businesses into a single Procurement & Supply Chain Services portfolio. The move brings together ProcureAbility, Retronix, ID8 Global, Velocity Electronics and Rebound Electronics under one operational structure.
The company operates more than 120 sites across the globe and employs 3,500 procurement and supply chain professionals. Jabil maintains relationships with more than 40,000
suppliers through its network
, providing customers with access to a broad range of sourcing options and procurement capabilities.
The engineering and manufacturing solutions provider acquired ProcureAbility and Retronix in 2023. ID8 Global was launched as a joint venture with Cyferd Inc in 2024. Velocity Electronics and Rebound Electronics were both acquired in 2025.

Inbound logistics remains one of the most labour-intensive and physically demanding nodes within global supply chain networks. Mobile robotics pioneer Boston Dynamics - a wholly-owned subsidiary of Hyundai Motor Group - has unveiled Stretch Gen 2, a next-generation autonomous mobile robot (AMR) specifically designed for warehouse activities, including trailer unloading.
Built upon
operational
data harvested from more than 100,000 industrial operating hours and tens of millions of handled cases, this second-generation platform introduces hardware, electrical, and structural upgrades designed to maximise unit availability, and improve dock-door throughput.

Walmart and Zipline have signed a multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the US. The retailer expects the expansion of delivery capabilities to increase the efficiency of fulfilment operations for staff and customers.
The new multi-year agreement expands the scope of Walmart's existing collaboration with Zipline. The two companies have been working together on drone deliveries since 2021.

title: Octave Expands Industrial AI Offering After Cerebre Takeover

Octave Expands Industrial AI Offering After Cerebre Takeover
Prioritise Us
on Google
Octave is strengthening industrial AI insights with its acquisition of Cerebre. Credit: Getty Images
Octave Intelligence has acquired Cerebre, adding a contextual model to strengthen industrial AI insights, explains Jeff Robbins, CEO at Cerebre
For customers in industrial environments, such as the oil and gas sector, there is a business need for AI insights to improve
resilience and performance
across the supply chain.
However, the insights also have to draw on expertise based on real-world conditions in order to be reliable.
Octave is responding to this need through its acquisition of Cerebre, which will broaden the scope and improve the accessibility of its industrial AI tools for its customers.
Supply chain transformation
Octave, a global leader in mission-critical software, has announced its acquisition of Cerebre. Cerebre is a US-based software company that uses its technological capabilities to transform fragmented engineering schematics, plant data and engineering knowledge into a connected model.
Octave is a technology company which helps organisations make informed decisions across the entire asset lifecycle. Through this, it ensures performance, safety and reliability are interwoven throughout the entire process.
Cerebre’s model means that any AI system, agent or engineer can make informed decisions from real plant knowledge, acting as the contact layer above raw data. This is particularly critical in the engineering sector, as it acts as one of the first steps in a
physical supply chain.
“Our customers run facilities where being wrong is not an option,” explains Mattias Stenberg, Chief Executive Officer of Octave.
Mattias Stenberg, Chief Executive Officer of Octave
“For years we have been building the record to design, build, operate and protect those facilities from one connected view. Cerebre provides insights into existing facilities, serving as a context engine for a unified plant model. Introducing Cerebre to Octave’s installed base, which covers 60% of Fortune 500 companies, supports our strategy of accelerated Annualised Recurring Revenue (ARR) growth and new licensing models.”
At a glance
Octave solutions are purpose-built for the domain
It makes use of context driven AI
Octave has a total revenue of US$415m - a 6% year-over-year increase
The company reports an 18% SaaS revenue growth since the year prior
Octave’s Data-as-a-Service has saved customers hundreds of work hours per year
Reducing fragmentation
Octave understands what its customers need, having the engineering system and record of each design. Major companies in the oil and gas sectors use Cerebre to place plant configuration, conditions and real-time knowledge in one process. This helps the plant maintain operations as it changes with external shifts.
Cerebre’s model begins with the plant, building off the context provided to the model in order to
develop a tailored solution
. Engineers can capture and govern plant-specific data which is often siloed, which then is used to explore how each team operates.
When combined with Octave’s AI applications and customer base, Cerebre helps shorten time to action and continues to operate alongside existing tools.
“We’ve spent years operating in stealth, pushing our technology to the limits with the world’s largest and most demanding operators,” says Jeff Robbins, Chief Executive Officer of Cerebre.
Jeff Robbins, Chief Executive Officer of Cerebre
“We built Cerebre so engineers and AI can reason over the same trusted, real-time model of the plant. By joining Octave, we are positioned to underpin industrial AI and expand across our combined customer base and beyond.”
Octave’s customer base will be able to have access to Cerebre’s capabilities, increasing the efficiency of the engineering and operations solutions. As the acquisition develops, further details will explore how global supply chains can benefit from this union.
Our customers run facilities where being wrong is not an option.
Mattias Stenberg, Chief Executive Officer of Octave
Key Partners
Octave delivers mission-critical software enabling organizations to make informed decisions throughout the asset lifecycle-Design, Build, Operate, and Protect. The platform transforms complex operational data into actionable intelligence, connecting expertise with real-world conditions and enterprise insights. Octave enhances performance, resilience, and incident response in environments where safety, reliability, and performance are essential and failure is unacceptable.
Cerebre builds context infrastructure for industrial AI operations. While engineers use plant knowledge to reason-equipment relationships, flow, control logic-AI systems need the same structured understanding. Cerebre creates and maintains this contextual model layer, enabling AI agents to reason over real plant knowledge rather than raw data.

title: Tesla Cybercab's autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn't move
content:
Tesla Robotaxi
Tesla Cybercab
Fred Lambert
| Nov 14 2026 - 5:33 am PT
Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.
And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.
What Cybercab owners agree to
The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company
started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use
at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.
The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.
Here’s what else is in there:
Tesla can change the subscription price with one month’s notice. You pay $29,990 up front, and the car’s usefulness then depends on a monthly fee Tesla sets.
The Cybercab only works inside Tesla-enabled Robotaxi geofences. Driving outside them is prohibited and can be technically blocked, and Tesla “may expand, reduce, relocate, or otherwise modify the operating area at any time.”
Tesla can suspend or cancel the subscription for “unauthorized or inappropriate use.” Three or more “strikeouts” for improper or unsafe use trigger a one-week suspension of autonomous driving, during which the car may not operate. Your payment isn’t prorated.
Tesla can remotely access, locate, restrict, or control the car, place it in a “safe state,” or end your access, and the agreement says those actions don’t give you remedies beyond what’s in the terms.
Tesla collects “Autonomy Data,” including image data from the cabin camera above the rear-view mirror, kept for 30 days by default.
It’s for personal use only. You can’t put your Cybercab on Tesla’s Robotaxi network, Uber, a delivery app, or a rental platform without Tesla’s written authorization.
No wraps, tint, or wheel changes except through Tesla or an authorized provider, or your subscription can be suspended.
That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.
Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was
between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps
, and parts of the Houston map have been
called “fake” by the person tracking it
. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.
Mark Valorian, who went through the terms
, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.
Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.
Tesla says the Model Y runs the same thing
This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.
Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network
around Q2 2027
. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.
So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.
Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.
Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.
Electrek’s Take
I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.
You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.
And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.
A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.
So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

title: I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike
content:
Micah Toll
| Nov 14 2026 - 5:02 am PT
I’ve been
waiting years
for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.
Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.
When it debuted earlier this year
, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.
USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare.
Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it
barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model
that’s slowly starting to ship.
The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition.
, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.
Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.
And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.
Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.
If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.
Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.
Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.
The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.
I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.
It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.
And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.
Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.
But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.
I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.
But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.
For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.
Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

title: First attempt to address screen printing-induced degradation in copper-plated heterojunction solar cells - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in China have investigated a previously overlooked degradation mechanism in copper-plated heterojunction solar cells caused by screen-printed photoresist. They found that progressive wear of the screen mesh can damage the cells’ passivation layers and reduce efficiency. An optimized emulsion buffer layer reportedly prevented the degradation over 40,000 consecutive printing cycles.
Emiliano Bellini
14 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
A heterojunction solar cell in testing
Screen printing is widely used in solar cell metallization, but the process can cause degradation that adversely affects device performance. The issue is particularly relevant for copper-plated silicon heterojunction (HJT) solar cells, which offer a promising route to reducing metallization costs and reliance on expensive silver.
The mechanical pressure and thermal treatments involved in screen printing can damage the sensitive passivating contact structures of HJT solar cells, increasing recombination losses and reducing conversion efficiency. Understanding the underlying degradation mechanisms is therefore essential to optimizing metallization processes without compromising cell performance.
Researchers in China have investigated the mechanisms behind screen printing-induced degradation in copper-plated HJT solar cells and developed a method to mitigate the effects, potentially improving their suitability for large-scale manufacturing.
“The screen-printing process for photoresist application in HJT cells differs fundamentally from conventional screen printing of silver paste,” corresponding author Lang Zhou told
pv magazine
. “In silver paste printing, the screen openings account for only 2–5% of the total area, while the remaining surface is covered by an emulsion layer that prevents direct contact between the mesh and the wafer. In contrast, full-area photoresist coating typically uses a screen without emulsion coverage to ensure uniform resist deposition across the entire wafer surface. As a result, the mesh comes into direct and extensive contact with the wafer during each printing cycle.”
The researchers said previous investigations had revealed a gradual decline in conversion efficiency from 26.2% to 25.7% over 15,000 consecutive printing cycles in commercial solar cell production. The losses were mainly attributed to reductions in open-circuit voltage and fill factor, while short-circuit current density and electrical resistance remained largely unchanged. Further measurements showed that minority carrier lifetime degradation increased from 0.61% with a new screen to 11.0% after 15,000 printing cycles.
The scientists used three-dimensional confocal microscopy to identify progressive wear of the screen mesh knuckles as the main cause of the degradation. As the knuckles wore down, their contact area with the wafer increased, placing greater mechanical stress on the underlying passivation layers. Although scanning electron microscopy revealed no visible surface scratches, photoluminescence measurements confirmed increased recombination losses, suggesting damage to the sensitive amorphous silicon/crystalline silicon interface.
To address the issue, the researchers developed an emulsion buffer layer to prevent direct contact between the screen mesh and the wafer surface. They evaluated six different patterns, with emulsion coverage ratios ranging from 2.9% to 16.6%.
The results showed a trade-off between mechanical protection and photoresist coating uniformity, as higher emulsion coverage reduced damage but impaired ink distribution. An emulsion coverage ratio of 4.7% provided the best balance, limiting minority carrier lifetime degradation to 0.41% after 10,000 printing cycles while maintaining relatively good coating uniformity.
The researchers attributed the improvement to the emulsion layer preventing direct contact between the screen mesh and the wafer surface, thereby reducing cumulative mechanical damage to the sensitive passivation layers.
“The findings demonstrate that a relatively simple modification to screen design can substantially mitigate printing-induced degradation, offering a practical approach to improving the manufacturing reliability of copper-plated HJT solar cells,” Zhou said.
The researchers presented their findings in “
Screen-printing photoresist induced efficiency degradation and mitigation in Cu-plated SHJ solar cells
,” published in
Solar Energy
The development comes amid growing interest in copper metallization as an alternative to silver-based contacts in HJT solar cells. In April 2026, researchers at China’s Nankai University
developed a silver-free HJT solar cell with 25.2% efficiency
using plasma-induced interface engineering and copper electroplating. The approach addressed adhesion, contact resistance and stability challenges at the ITO interface, highlighting the potential of copper-based metallization for high-efficiency devices. pv magazine Global
In a separate development, scientists at Germany’s Forschungszentrum Jülich
achieved 23.08% efficiency in a fully copper-metallized HJT solar cell
. The silver-free device exhibited a relatively small efficiency penalty compared with its silver-metallized counterpart, while cells combining silver-copper paste on the front side with silver contacts on the rear reached 23.95% efficiency. The findings underline the potential of copper to reduce silver consumption, although further improvements in processing and electrical performance remain necessary. pv magazine Global

title: Great Lakes irradiance surges as wet weather weighs on Southwest solar resource - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a new weekly update for pv magazine,
, a DNV company, reports that North American solar irradiance was 0.8% above average in October 2026, with the Northeast and Great Lakes recording a 14% surplus and record highs in Buffalo and Cleveland. Meanwhile, heavy rainfall and persistent cloud cover pushed irradiance 9% below normal across the Southwest and northern Mexico, with Phoenix recording its second-lowest October level.
14 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
North American irradiance remained close to normal overall in October, but the continental average concealed sharply contrasting conditions for solar assets. Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) was 0.8% above normal across North America, while the Great Lakes and Northeast recorded substantial
irradiance surpluses and the Southwest and northern Mexico experienced widespread deficits during an unusually wet month, according to analysis using the
Solcast API
Across the Northeast and Great Lakes, October GHI averaged 14% above normal, with 95.5% of the region recording above-average irradiance. The largest anomalies occurred around Upstate New York and parts of Michigan, where GHI was approximately 20-25% above normal. Higher atmospheric pressure, lower humidity and below-normal precipitation across much of the region reduced the frequency of cloudy periods, allowing more solar radiation to reach the surface. Buffalo recorded the strongest October GHI in its 2007-2026 series, illustrating the scale of the regional surplus.
Cleveland experienced a similarly exceptional month, with its average daily profile also setting a high for the city in the Solcast record.
These conditions were particularly relevant across the Northeast, where significant volumes of distributed solar are installed in states including New York, New Jersey and Massachusetts.
Conditions were markedly different farther southwest. A strong low-pressure trough approaching the West Coast drew Pacific moisture into the Four Corners where Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah meet. Moisture associated with Tropical Storms Polo and Trudy, also contributed to several days of heavy rainfall throughout the month of October. The San Luis Valley received more than four times its usual October rainfall in four days, while the San Juan River at Pagosa Springs reached its second-highest crest since 1911.
Elevated atmospheric moisture extended across much of the Southwest and northern Mexico, increasing cloud cover and coinciding with a broad irradiance deficit. GHI across the region averaged 9% below the October norm. Phoenix recorded GHI approximately 10% below its 2007-2025 October average, making October 2026 the second-lowest October for GHI in the Solcast record.
The below-normal conditions covered the solar-intensive corridor from Southern California into Arizona, exposing a substantial concentration of utility-scale solar assets to the same regional irradiance deficit.
produces these figures by tracking clouds and aerosols at 1-2km resolution globally, using satellite data and proprietary
AI/ML algorithms
. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.

title: UNSW develops three-minute lithium-ion battery health test - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers at the University of New South Wales (UNSW) have developed a prototype that uses electrical pulses and statistical models to assess lithium-ion battery health in under three minutes per cell, with a potential role in sorting retired batteries for reuse or recycling.
Ev Foley
14 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
UNSW researchers in Sydney have developed a prototype battery health test that they said is 95.5% faster and more than 80% cheaper than existing methods, with potential to increase second-life battery use and keep battery waste out of landfill.
The platform is designed to work with the management systems already used by recyclers and energy storage operators, and to assess the three main lithium-ion chemistries used in electric vehicles and energy storage: lithium iron phosphate (LFP), nickel cobalt aluminum (NCA), and nickel manganese cobalt (NMC).
Current testing of used batteries relies on a full charge-discharge cycle of about 10 hours, which can lead to overheating and fire if damaged batteries endure hours of high-stress cycling, according to the researchers. It costs about AUD 120 ($85) per EV battery pack.
The UNSW prototype instead sends short electrical pulses through each cell and measures how it responds. Statistical models then estimate the battery’s health in under three minutes per cell, with lab tests showing more than 90% accuracy, the researchers said. They are targeting a cost of under AUD 25.
Huadong Mo, an associate professor at UNSW’s School of Systems and Computing, said that as more EVs reach the end of their life, Australia has a real opportunity to build a local second-life battery industry, with retired batteries supporting grid and community energy storage.
“Up to 95% of a battery’s components can be recovered, some even to make new batteries. Yet only a small fraction of lithium-ion batteries in Australia are collected for recycling today,” Mo said.
Field trials
The researchers have partnered with Malaysia-headquartered battery recycling and lifecycle management company DY New Energy on an AUD 1.3 million project to test the technology on more than 500 batteries in real-world conditions.
Before piloting it in recycling facilities and second-life storage systems, DY New Energy and UNSW will develop and test a machine-learning decision engine that recommends whether retired batteries should be reused or recycled. A battery management system module, called iBMS, will then feed those insights directly into battery systems for real-time monitoring and decision support.
Ziyang Lyu, research lead at UNSW’s School of Mathematics and Statistics, said recyclers rarely receive neatly sorted batches.
“One day it might be LFP cells, the next a mix of nickel-based chemistries from different manufacturers. We’ve designed our models to handle that variety, so the platform works with the batteries operators actually receive, not just ideal lab samples,” Lyu said.
Lyu said the technology could also help manage the growing number of batteries in stationary storage. “This technology could also support the future reuse and recycling of Australia’s rapidly expanding fleet of stationary energy storage systems, contributing to a more sustainable and circular battery economy,” he said.
The project is also supported by the Trailblazer for Recycling and Clean Energy (TRaCE) Lab to Market Fund. On Nov. 13, DY New Energy said it will partner with the Australian Research Council’s Fire Resilience Infrastructure, Assets and Safety Advancements (FRIASA) Hub to advance safe and scalable battery recycling.

title: 'The times I regret are the ones when I didn’t value myself enough to speak up' - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
This week Women in Solar+ Europe gives voice to Tracey Elliott, Director of UK-based Eden Sustainable Power. She says increasing female representation through role models, mentorship, and inclusive workplaces is essential, alongside empowering women to bring their unique perspectives into leadership.
Women in Solar+ Europe
14 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Tracey Elliott
I believe every business benefits from diverse teams, and the evidence supports that. McKinsey’s 2023 report,
Diversity Matters Even More,
found that companies with the most gender-diverse executive teams were 39% more likely to outperform financially.
This matters especially in our industry. Technology, policy, the global picture and grid demands are shifting rapidly, so we need teams that can adapt. In my experience, diverse teams are exactly that. They spot problems faster and find ways through change. Yet women hold only 32% of renewable energy jobs, so we’re missing out on talent we need.
Leadership starts with who enters the industry
The scale of what we need to deliver is huge. The UK government’s Solar Roadmap aims for at least 45 GW of solar capacity by 2030, and its Clean Energy Jobs Plan expects around 400,000 additional clean energy jobs by then. We will not fill those roles by recruiting from the same, largely male, talent pool. Widening who we reach, through visible role models and by promoting the exciting careers on offer, brings in more talent. That’s what makes a sector resilient.
The biggest challenge is that the benefits are not always immediate or obvious, like a rise in sales figures. They build over time: wider talent pools, better working conditions, and creative teams with broader perspectives. The bigger prize is our sector meeting its skills challenge with homegrown talent. Microsoft research found girls were almost twice as likely to be interested in science, technology, engineering and maths when they had role models. When young people see people like them in solar, they can picture themselves there. Inclusion is how we grow our sector well.
Sadly, I’m yet to see the shifts we really need. I’m researching the barriers to completing electrical apprenticeships, and there’s still very little diversity on courses or out on site. Women make up just 11% of engineering and construction apprenticeship starts and only 14% of electrical and electronic engineering degree entrants. Leadership starts with that pipeline. We need to make these great careers more visible in schools and colleges and make construction sites good places for women to work.
Bring your difference to the table
The wonderful thing about moving into renewables as a woman in my fifties is that, frankly, I give far fewer sh**s about what people think. By this stage of life, you know who you are and what matters. For me, that means making a difference for our planet and the beautiful people who live on it. We need to decarbonise, do it quickly and make the transition fair. I want to be part of making that happen.
I’ve been incredibly lucky. My co-directors, Scott Burrows and Steve Baker, who co-founded Eden Sustainable and Eden Sustainable Power, believed in me, championed me and gave me opportunities. I came to solar later than they did, with less experience, and they were endlessly patient with my questions. They helped fast-track me into leadership, and I’m so grateful to lead alongside them.
I’ve never had a formal mentor, but I’ve learned so much from my co-directors and friends. We’ve been each other’s sounding boards, sharing challenges and mistakes. I’ve also worked part-time for years as a palliative care specialist nurse, where we had regular psychotherapy. I was sceptical, but now I’d recommend knowing yourself better to everyone. If you don’t have a mentor, I’d encourage you to find your people and learn together.
Be passionate, be enthusiastic and be keen to learn. Dig in, put the time in and, when you don’t understand something, speak up and ask questions. Be prepared, then be even more prepared. I need to take my own advice on that one, but I know that’s when I’m at my best. Take a deep breath and bring your difference to the table. The times I regret are the ones when I didn’t value myself enough to speak up.
Give talent somewhere to take root
For me, an inclusive culture starts with leading by example. Treat people as you would want to be treated, and encourage the team to do the same. The best thing we did at Eden was talk about our values as a team and get clear about what we all wanted together. That way, everyone owns those values, lives them and holds each other accountable. We make sure everyone can tell us when things aren’t landing and help shape how we do better. Culture needs time and care, yet it’s often the first thing to go when you’re busy, or money is tight. So we need to protect it.
The most gorgeous impact has been watching flexible working take hold across our teams. Men and women alike can regularly do their share of school runs, school plays, sports days and dentist appointments. I’ve watched family life flourish as a result, and we’ve seen the benefits in our team feedback. That started with a leadership team who understood those pressures from the inside and modelled what we value.
In Solar Energy UK’s skills working party, we’ve been talking about how talent and teams grow best in fertile soil. If we want young people, women and people from diverse backgrounds to build careers in solar, our sites and teams have to be places where they want to work and can thrive. We created Solar Energy UK’s Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Toolkit to give smaller, busy companies simple steps to get started. Get the soil right, and the talent will take root and stay.
There’s a place for you in solar
To a young woman entering solar, I’d say this is a brilliant sector to work in. You’ll go home knowing you’re making a difference, helping our economy decarbonise and bringing health benefits for people and planet, now and for future generations. There are bonus opportunities too, from building things that last to recycling and encouraging nature around solar sites.
With a creaking grid and unstable global markets, we need people who are creative, flexible and quick on their feet. There’s never a dull moment, and there’s plenty of room to grow. Whatever your personality, there’s a place for you in this sector, from working on the tools to finance and everything in between.
Tracey Elliott is a Director at Eden Sustainable Power, where she is committed to accelerating the UK’s transition to a cleaner, more electrified future through renewable energy and private energy markets, helping consumers and generators realise the value of renewables. She combines commercial expertise with a strong focus on stakeholder engagement, skills development and industry collaboration. Tracey is Co-Chair of the Solar Energy UK Skills Working Party, helping to tackle workforce challenges and improve diversity across the sector. She speaks regularly at national energy events and has been recognised for promoting careers and inclusion in the green economy. She is Co-Founder and Trustee of The Pickwell Foundation, which works on climate change and on supporting people displaced by conflict and disaster. Tracey co-owns Pickwell Manor and Ravendere Retreats, luxury sustainable holiday accommodation and a retreat venue in North Devon.

title: Masdar completes $950 million solar and battery storage project in California - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The Abu Dhabi clean energy developer and its joint venture partner Terra-Gen have brought the Lockhart complex online, adding 365 MW of solar generation and 173.7 MW of energy storage to the California grid.
Ryan Kennedy
14 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
Vista aérea de una central solar en el Valle de California.
Abu Dhabi clean energy company Masdar has announced the completion of its $950 million Lockhart Solar and Storage complex in California, adding significant utility-scale generation and grid-stability assets to the U.S. market.
Developed by Terra-Gen, which is jointly owned by Masdar and Igneo Infrastructure Partners, the facility features 365 MW of solar photovoltaic generation paired with 173.7 MW of battery energy storage systems. Combined, the installation is designed to generate enough electricity to meet the annual needs of approximately 350,000 homes and businesses.
The multi-year construction effort drove substantial localized economic activity across the region. Over a four-year development span, the project supported more than 1,000 peak on-site construction jobs and accumulated roughly 880,000 working hours. Over its operational lifecycle, the facility is projected to deliver upwards of $40 million in local property tax revenue alongside direct community benefit funds. Commercially, the project is backed by a hybrid of long-term power purchase agreements with California load-serving entities and corporate offtake agreements.
The milestone underscores Masdar’s aggressive growth trajectory in the United States, where it has already invested approximately $3 billion. Backed by its shareholders TAQA, ADNOC, and Mubadala, the company plans to inject an additional $20 billion into the U.S. market over the coming decade.
Masdar is targeting an expansion of its U.S. renewable energy portfolio to as much as 25 GW by 2030, driven heavily by surging power demand from commercial data centers, industrial electrification, and domestic manufacturing load growth. Globally, the Abu Dhabi clean energy powerhouse continues scaling toward a 100 GW portfolio capacity target by the end of the decade.
