title: Clarifying the CATL Tener Sodium, with new specifications and availability - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
New specs for CATL’s four-hour sodium-ion battery reveal how the company will market the product for cost benefits over LFP-based batteries. International deliveries are due to begin in summer 2027.
Tristan Rayner
14 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
CATL’s Tener Sodium battery energy storage system (BESS) is one of the most anticipated new products on the market, as markets watch for the great hope to compete with lithium-ion products across a number of potential scenarios.
The Tener Sodium product launched at The Smarter E event 2026 in Munich in June, and at the time, the company gave a capacity of more than 30 MWh per block.
With further details scarce, a Oct. 29 ATA Insights webinar hosted CATL energy storage product solution manager David Santiago showed specficiations and datasheets across the BESS and in-house PCS to detail how the four-hour system comes together.
The system is built in pairs, with two, four, six or eight cabinets available to spec. The full block sits in two back-to-back rows of four and measures 18.2 m across, 7 m deep and 3.5 m high.
Santiago put each cabinet at around 15 feet long and 44 to 45 metric tons. That works out to about 4 MWh per cabinet in the eight-cabinet version.
At launch, CATL had put the module weight at about 42 metric tons. CATL also plans to use the same cabinets and layout for a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) version. Santiago put that version at around 50 MWh across eight cabinets and said developers could choose the chemistry during project design. CATL is prioritizing sodium-ion certification, with the LFP version to follow.
Tener Sodium: Core battery specs
The provided system specifications lists a rated energy of 30+ MWh, with a charge and discharge rate of up to 0.25P, or a power output of 7.5 MW for four hours. (Santiago didn’t specify a power output change if the block has a final capacity of 32 MWh)
The battery is rated at 1,166.88 V DC, with a voltage range of 612 V to 1,387.2 V. CATL specifies 95% round-trip efficiency at 25°C and 0.25P, and 70% state of health after 20 years under a 0.25P duty cycle marked “1cls” on the slide.
The liquid-cooled battery operates from −35°C to +55°C and can be stored from −35°C to +60°C. CATL lists noise at 65 dB(A) or less, IP55 ingress protection, C5 corrosion protection with C4 optional, and operation up to 4,000 m without derating. Communications include CAN, Modbus TCP/IP and RS485.
At launch, CATL reported 15,000 cycles at 25°C and more than 10,000 at 45°C, as well as more than 92% capacity retention at −20°C. The liquid-cooled battery operates from −35°C to +55°C. It is rated IP55, with operation up to 4,000 m without derating.
PCS: CATL’s own in-house Terapower 265 kW converter
CATL uses bidirectional DC/DC conversion to boost voltage at the low end of the battery’s range. The Terapower module shown in the webinar combines that DC/DC stage with a power conversion system (PCS). CATL offers its own PCS though it can also work with other manufacturers.
It takes 600 V to 1,500 V DC at up to 222 A and is rated at 265 kW, with a 690 V AC output at 50 or 60 Hz. CATL lists peak efficiency of at least 99.2%, full-load efficiency of at least 98.5% and current harmonic distortion below 3% at rated load.
The converter is liquid-cooled and rated IP66, with an operating range of −40°C to +60°C and a maximum altitude of 5,000 m. It starts to derate above 50°C and above 3,000 m. It lists RS485, Ethernet and CAN interfaces and support for IEC 61850 and Modbus TCP.
Santiago said the PCS ties into the battery’s thermal management system and is accounted for in its auxiliary consumption.
Tener Sodium c
ooling, auxiliary power, cycling
vs CATL’s LFP EnerX
Against its EnerX 0.25P LFP system, CATL says the sodium-ion cells generate 27.2% less heat per unit of energy at the beginning of life and 32.7% less at end of life.
For a 50 MWh station, it puts DC-side refrigeration capacity at 490 kW, down from 720 kW for EnerX. It lists noise at 65 dB(A) versus 75 dB(A) and puts the share of power used by auxiliaries 10% lower. At launch, CATL separately put Tener Sodium’s auxiliary consumption at 1%, against what it called a 2% industry average.
The spec sheet lists 95% round-trip efficiency at 25°C and 0.25P and 70% state of health after 20 years at one cycle per day. The webinar’s degradation curves put capacity retention at 71.3% after 20 years at one cycle per day and 65.2% after 19 years at two cycles per day. Santiago described those curves as older estimates and said CATL had since obtained “better” data as the product matures.
Cost savings and f
ootprint
For a 500 MWh project, CATL modeled 16 Tener Sodium blocks against 23 EnerX blocks. The sodium layout covered 6,630 m², compared with about 9,700 m² for EnerX, a reduction of roughly 32%.
In CATL’s comparison, a Tener Sodium block takes up 158.5 m², against 180.6 m² for an EnerX 0.25P LFP block. The slide lists an areal density of 0.197 MWh/m² for Tener Sodium and 0.125 MWh/m² for EnerX.
In terms of cost savings overall in this scenario, CATL estimated 9.2% lower engineering, procurement and construction costs for the sodium layout.
Of that breakdown, EPC equipment costs fell 12%, civil works excluding labor fell 16%, and labor fell 17% in the model. CATL used the same design and management fees for both layouts. The fine print notes the estimate excludes transport, the substation and what CATL labels “DC/AC side” costs. In addition, CATL has several other LFP-based products, including its Tener Stack, that likely competes far better with the Tener Sodium.
Referring again to the presentation, the eight module Tener Sodium block again measures to be 18.2 m across, 7 m deep and 3.5 m high. Santiago noted, however, each sodium cabinet was said to be “15ft” in size. However, at 3.5 m high, this would exceed the height of a standard high-cube shipping container.
Availability
While already being delivered in China, CATL gave an overseas delivery window in the webinar for summer 2027, after the August 2027 production window, though the shipping method and cost remain open.
Santiago noted CATL is receiving “a lot of orders.”

title: Transparent bamboo boosts energy performance of solar PV skylights - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Researchers tested 21 glazing configurations using transparent wood and PV modules with different transparency levels. Bamboo-based systems achieved the lowest heat gain and cooling operating costs.
Lior Kahana
14 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Cells & modules
Illustration of the device
A research team from India’s
Vellore Institute of Technology
has designed and tested a glazing system that combines transparent wood (TW) with transparent solar PV (TSPV) modules. Transparent wood is produced by removing light-absorbing lignin from wood and filling the resulting porous structure with a transparent polymer.
“The proposed system comprises two layers: a TSPV panel layer, which generates electricity while maintaining transparency, and a second layer of TW, which would remain transparent and blocks heat gain in the interior portion of the building,” the researchers said. “A thorough investigation was conducted to assess the impacts of these materials on heat gain and illuminance through experimental analysis.”
The researchers tested the proposed system as skylight glazing. They fabricated transparent wood from 1 mm-thick veneers of balsa, poplar, and pine, as well as bamboo. They removed the lignin through chemical treatment before vacuum-infiltrating the remaining structures with transparent epoxy resin.
The researchers then combined the samples with commercially sourced PV modules featuring nominal transparency levels of 0%, 20%, 40%, and 60%. They evaluated 21 configurations, including PV modules without transparent wood and an 8 mm-thick clear-glass reference. The tests involved small cardboard building models measuring 12.5 cm on each side, with a 5.5 cm × 5.5 cm skylight opening.
Halogen lamps simulated hourly solar irradiance calculated for Vellore’s climate, while heat-flux sensors and a lux meter measured heat gain and indoor illuminance. The researchers repeated the heat-gain measurements four times and extrapolated representative-day results across the March-to-October cooling season. They then calculated cooling costs and avoided emissions based on an air-conditioning coefficient of performance (COP) of 3.5, an electricity tariff of $0.08/kWh, and an emissions factor of 0.98 kg CO2/kWh.
“Bamboo emerged as the most effective material in combining with TSPV, achieving the lowest heat gain at all levels of transparency, even at 60%, it has shown 371.78 kWh/m² and exhibited effective cost saving of 20.32 $/m²/year,” the researchers said. “Moreover, it has intense power in mitigating carbon emissions, and it has mitigated as much as 0.058 tCO2/year per annum for the PV module with 60% nominal transparency combined with transparent bamboo.”
The results showed that integrating transparent wood slightly reduced cooling energy demand, with PV modules combined with transparent bamboo consistently recording the lowest operating costs among the TSPV glazing configurations.
“Because of reduced transparencies in 0% and 20%, the operating cost, cost savings and CO2 emission mitigations show similar values to the baseline TSPV glazing systems,” the researchers said.
They presented their findings in “
Transparent wood integrated with transparent solar photovoltaic panels for enhanced building energy performance and economic benefits
,” which was recently published in
Scientific Reports

title: Yanhe Technology launches three perovskite solar module technologies into orbit - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Beijing-based Yanhe Technology has launched three perovskite-based photovoltaic modules into low Earth orbit to assess their performance under space conditions. The mission will test perovskite-silicon tandem, perovskite-CIGS tandem, and flexible single-junction perovskite technologies.
Vincent Shaw
14 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Yanhe Technology launched three independently developed space photovoltaic modules into a 535 km sun-synchronous orbit aboard Galactic Energy’s Ceres-2 Y3 rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on Nov. 7. The company described the mission as China’s first simultaneous in-orbit validation of three perovskite-based PV technologies.
Two tandem modules – a perovskite-crystalline silicon device and a perovskite-CIGS device – are installed on the North University of China-1 satellite. The spacecraft operates in a dawn-dusk orbit, where near-continuous sunlight places demanding requirements on power density and long-term stability.
A flexible single-junction perovskite module is installed on the Yunyao-1 28 satellite. The device will undergo imaging during thermal cycling and performance monitoring to assess degradation caused by particle radiation and atomic oxygen exposure.
Yanhe has not disclosed the conversion efficiencies, rated power outputs, active areas, or weights of the three modules. The company had not responded to a request for additional technical specifications at the time of publication. Yanhe’s official announcement and independent industry reports confirmed the launch, satellite platforms, and orbital altitude.
The mission builds on an earlier in-orbit testing campaign launched in September, when Yanhe deployed a flexible perovskite module aboard the Tianyi-52 satellite for long-term performance monitoring. The company described that deployment as China’s first component-level in-orbit test of flexible perovskite PV technology.
In October, Yanhe also established a joint laboratory with the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology to conduct research on perovskite solar cells, space photovoltaics, orbital energy systems, and flexible devices.
Yanhe Chief Technology Officer Peng Zongyang said the perovskite-silicon and perovskite-CIGS tandem architectures target different segments of the space PV market. He said the latest mission aims to evaluate the efficiency and stability of both technologies under actual orbital conditions.
The company is assessing the fully thin-film perovskite-CIGS tandem architecture for potential advantages in flexibility and radiation resistance over silicon-based tandem devices.
Perovskite solar cells have attracted interest for space applications because of their potential for high specific power and lower material costs compared with the III-V gallium arsenide solar cells commonly used in satellite power systems.
Yanhe is targeting the growing low Earth orbit satellite constellation market, where lighter PV modules could help reduce launch costs.
However, the ability of perovskite solar modules to maintain performance under prolonged radiation exposure and repeated thermal cycling remains a key technical challenge.
The latest mission is expected to generate comparative in-orbit performance data for the three architectures. Yanhe has not specified the duration of the monitoring campaign or the amount of telemetry data expected from the satellites.

title: When trackers don’t talk - pv magazine Global
content: When a single-axis tracker loses its wireless link to the plant controller, it doesn’t just drop off a dashboard. Depending on the failsafe, it can stop tracking, stall at a fixed angle, or fall out of a coordinated stow – each of which costs energy or means a technician must visit a remote row. On a plant with hundreds or thousands of trackers, communication reliability is a production and operations and maintenance (O&M) line item, not a networking footnote. Yet the radio layout is often one of the last things designed, and one of the least rigorously specified. The industry’s common approach is a rule of thumb, typically placing a gateway every few rows, keeping it close to the controller it serves, and trusting the Zigbee mesh communication protocol to fill in the gaps. That worked well enough on fixed-tilt sites. On trackers, it often breaks. Radio optimization A single-axis tracker is a large, moving assembly of metal – torque tubes, bearings, module frames, and the modules themselves – and metal reflects, absorbs, and diffracts the 2.4 GHz signals that Zigbee relies on. Crucially, that geometry is not static. As the rows rotate from a steep east-facing tilt at sunrise, through flat at midday, to a steep west-facing tilt at sunset, the radio environment moves with them. A link that is perfectly healthy at noon can degrade or drop entirely at high tilt angles early in the morning or late in the afternoon. This is precisely what rule-of-thumb design cannot capture. A static gateway count says ­nothing about how coverage shifts across the operating day, so networks that look fine on paper or during a midday commissioning check can go on to develop intermittent, angle-dependent faults that are notoriously difficult to reproduce and diagnose in the field. There is a second, less obvious obstacle. Most tracker control systems are built on off-the-shelf gateway hardware, which does not expose the low-level radio data needed to characterize any of this. Without direct access to what the radio chip actually sees on site – per-link signal strength, link quality, retransmissions – there is no empirical picture of how a mesh really behaves on a live tracker plant, and therefore no basis for anything better than guesswork and over-provisioning. This is why we made the deliberate choice to design our own gateway rather than integrate a commercial one. Reading the radio’s chip-level telemetry directly from plants in normal operation gave us something the industry has never really had: a large, real-world dataset of how 2.4 GHz signals actually propagate across tracker fields as the rows move. On top of that dataset we trained a machine-­learning model that predicts radio propagation as a function of the three variables that matter most on a tracker plant: the tilt angle of the panels, the type of structure or tracker, and the layout of the plant itself. The model has learned from several dozen sites representing several hundred megawatts of projects, spanning different tracker designs, plant configurations and terrain types. Rather than assuming a generic propagation environment, it adapts its predictions to the specific hardware and topography of each project. The output is a coverage map of the site that can be evaluated before a single gateway is installed, and – just as importantly – evaluated across the full range of tracker angles rather than at one convenient moment. Actionable simulation A propagation model is only useful if you can act on its recommendations. If the gateway is physically tied to the network control unit, its ­position is dictated by wherever that cabinet happens to sit – which may be nowhere near the RF-optimal location. In our architecture the gateways are deported from the main controller, so they can be placed wherever the simulation indicates coverage is strongest, independently of the controller’s position. The software identifies where the network wants a gateway and the hardware makes it possible to put it there. The clearest test of this approach is a retrofit at a project where the “before” is a real, underperforming network. We recently retrofitted the tracker control system on a portfolio of five operating plants in Europe, ranging from 5 MW to 23 MW – roughly 49 MW in total. The sites suffered from two chronic issues: control cabinets that were failing in the field, and communication dead zones – entire areas of the plants that lost their radio links as soon as the trackers tilted away from horizontal. We modelled each existing layout with our simulation tool, which immediately made the weak zones visible and explained why the original radio placement could never provide reliable coverage across the full tracking range. On one of the plants – an 11 MW site with around 340 trackers split into two zones – the incumbent architecture attached two gateways to each zone’s network control unit. Four gateways on paper, but only two radio locations in practice: pairs of radios stacked at the same points, their positions dictated by where the cabinets stood rather than by any analysis of coverage. Doubling the hardware at the wrong spot creates redundancy, not coverage – and the plant’s extremities, hundreds of meters from either cabinet, were precisely where the links dropped as the trackers tilted. In the retrofit, the simulation determined both how many deported gateways each zone actually required and exactly where to place them among the rows. Deployed at those computed positions, the network behaved as predicted from day one: the dead zones disappeared across the full range of tracker angles, with no field trial and error and nothing added after commissioning. That result is worth dwelling on. Radio problems on tracker plants are usually “solved” iteratively in the field – moving antennas, adding repeaters, chasing intermittent faults that only show up at certain tilt angles. Here, the layout was computed before deployment and worked as planned. The dead zones had existed for one reason only: the original radio points were positioned by the constraints of the cabinet and by habit, as they are on most plants today, with no empirical way of knowing how the signal would behave once thousands of square meters of steel started moving. Simulation replaced that guesswork with measured physics, and the problem disappeared. Engineering discipline Wireless communication on tracker plants is too tightly coupled to yield and O&M cost to keep designing it by intuition, and the data needed to do better already exists at the radio chip level of every plant – it just has to be collected and learned from. Measured, modeled, and validated against real propagation data, the radio layout becomes just another engineering parameter of the plant design: something a developer or EPC can specify, verify and guarantee up front, rather than discover in the field one tilted morning at a time. title: 5,000-year-old Chinese brewing secret: red mold, cloth lined filters
content: Brewers in China used red mold and bast-fiber textiles to filter rice-based alcoholic beverages approximately 5,000 years ago, according to a new study.University of Arizona researchers examined 16 pottery vessels and five specialized filters from the Wayaoli archaeological site in China’s Zhejiang Province. Using microscopic residue analysis, they identified starch grains, phytoliths, fungi, and microfibers preserved on the pottery. These residues indicated that the vessels were used to produce rice-based alcoholic beverages, including red-colored alcohol made with Monascus mold.Ancient brewers used red mold to ferment riceArchaeologists first found five unusual pottery filters with connected upper and lower bowls. Based on their design, they suspected they might have been used to produce alcohol, although it appeared they could also have supported other processes, including grain processing and water purification.However, residue analysis revealed rice starch and traces of Monascus mold, which is associated with traditional red rice brewing, on all five filters. Its enzymes break down rice starch into sugars that can then be fermented, the study reported. Additionally, the mold produces red pigments, suggesting that the Ancient Chinese drank red alcohol.Some starch grains showed damage consistent with cooking and fermentation, providing further evidence that the vessels were used in alcohol production. Researchers also discovered several starchy plant fibers, including foxnut, Job’s tears, and underground storage organs.The residue evidence aligns with an earlier study conducted at the Shangshan archaeological site in Zhejiang Province, dating back 10,000–9,000 years, which indicated that Monascus was used to ferment rice-based beverages. Another processing techniqueResearchers found traces of microscopic fibers identified as bast-fibers, which stem from the inner bark of plant stems and can be used to manufacture textiles.That suggests ancient brewers placed woven fabric inside the upper bowls of the pottery filters to separate the liquid from solid material.“These bast fibers were likely woven into textiles and placed on the upper filter bowl to improve alcohol filtration,” said researchers.The study states that bast-fiber textiles were used for filtration, improving both the taste and clarity of alcoholic beverages. However, researchers found no intact cloth at the archaeological site.Alcohol held ritual significanceAccording to the study, most of these pottery filters came from burials excavated at the site.These vessels frequently appeared alongside other pottery associated with household activities, including jars, plates, and cooking pots.The researchers interpreted the presence of filters in burials as evidence of alcohol’s importance in the community’s social and ritual traditions.Late Neolithic societies in the Lower Yangzi River region were known for their intensive rice agriculture, technological innovation that increased social complexity, and elaborate ritual practices. Rice fermentation played a role in advancing culture and manufacturing techniques. By analyzing the microscopic residues on ancient pottery, researchers uncovered a major feature of these cultures. They identified evidence of both fermentation and filtration techniques used about five millennia ago.The study findings demonstrated the production of rice-based fermented beverages using Monascus molds and bast-fiber textiles. It suggested the significance of alcohol during the social and rituals during the Late Songze and Early Liangzhu periods.

title: Water-based battery keeps nearly all its capacity over 1,000 cycles
content: A water-based zinc-iodine battery held on to nearly all its storage capacity after thousands of charge and discharge cycles in lab tests led by University College London (UCL). The researchers developed an electrolyte that keeps reactive forms of iodine stable in water, allowing the battery to draw more capacity from the same material.The study tackles a problem that has limited the use of water-based batteries in large energy storage projects. These batteries offer a potential alternative to lithium-ion systems, which can pose a fire risk, but their relatively low energy density makes it harder to store large amounts of electricity.Getting more capacity from iodineThe team’s design allows iodine to transfer 4 electrons during charging and discharging, up from 2 in conventional iodine battery chemistry. That gives the battery access to more of iodine’s storage capacity. The difficulty is keeping the highly reactive forms of iodine that emerge along the way from reacting with water.Earlier experiments addressed this problem with highly concentrated electrolytes containing halogens. Those mixtures helped stabilize iodine but were corrosive and costly, making them difficult to manufacture at scale. The UCL-led team changed the chemistry of the liquid immediately surrounding the iodine. Some molecules in the new electrolyte keep water away, while others bind to reactive forms of iodine and help prevent unwanted reactions.Putting the chemistry through thousands of cyclesThe researchers demonstrated the electrolyte in both pouch and coin cells. Pouch cells are the flat packages commonly used in phones and laptops. Coin cells are small, disk-shaped batteries typically used in devices with lower power demands. The chemistry worked in both formats.In separate durability tests, the zinc-iodine cells kept nearly all their initial storage capacity after thousands of cycles. That matters for grid storage, where batteries must repeatedly absorb surplus electricity from wind and solar farms and release it when generation drops.The researchers said the electrolyte design could also be adapted for aluminum-iodine batteries, giving them another chemistry to explore for stationary storage.Taking the battery beyond the labLarge battery farms currently rely on lithium-ion technology. Water-based designs could give grid operators another option, but the team still needs to test its electrolyte in larger systems and see how the cells behave under operating conditions closer to those of a battery farm. Those tests would help determine how well the capacity and durability observed in the lab carry over to a larger installation.“I am excited that our new chemistry can help aqueous batteries move one step closer to commercialization and wide deployment. Next steps include testing this technology at a larger scale and improving its performance under realistic operating conditions,” said Guanjie He, a professor at UCL Chemistry and the study’s corresponding author.First author Ruwei Chen said the work also points to a broader challenge in designing rechargeable iodine batteries. “We also need to understand how they interact with the water-based electrolyte and how those interactions change as the battery charges and discharges,” he said.The study was published in the Nature journal.

title: US' top nuclear rivals expand undersea capabilities, add new submarines
content: The United States Navy is facing a growing challenge beneath the ocean’s surface, with China rapidly expanding its nuclear-powered submarine fleet and Russia continuing to invest in advanced underwater weapons and strategic missile submarines.Rear Adm. Chris Cavanaugh, commander of Submarine Forces, US Pacific Fleet (COMSUBPAC), outlined the growing threat during the Navy Submarine League’s 2026 Annual Symposium. His assessment highlighted not only the increasing number of adversary submarines but also improvements in their capabilities, supporting infrastructure, and underwater surveillance networks.China is building submarines at an accelerating paceAccording to Naval News, which reported on Cavanaugh’s presentation on November 13, the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) has brought eight Type 093B, or Shang III, nuclear-powered attack submarines into service in less than four years. Cavanaugh said US assessments indicate that Chinese shipyards could sustain a similar production pace for at least another decade, potentially adding 20 to 40 Shang III or improved submarines during that period.The USNI News report on Cavanaugh’s remarks also highlighted his warning that China’s growing submarine numbers are being accompanied by improvements in individual vessel capabilities.The Shang III represents a significant step up from earlier Chinese nuclear attack submarines. Cavanaugh pointed to improved acoustic quieting, propulsion changes, and 24 vertical launch cells that could accommodate missiles. He suggested that the scale of these changes makes the Shang III effectively a new submarine class rather than a simple upgrade.China is also developing the Type 095 nuclear-powered guided-missile submarine and the Type 096 ballistic missile submarine, which would strengthen its sea-based nuclear deterrent. The latter is particularly important to China’s second-strike capability: the ability to retaliate with nuclear weapons even after an initial attack.China’s undersea ambitions extend beyond submarinesCavanaugh also highlighted China’s growing investment in oceanographic research, seabed mapping, unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs), and supporting infrastructure.These activities could give Chinese submarines a better understanding of underwater conditions, including ocean currents, temperature layers, and seabed geography. Such information can influence how submarines navigate, conceal themselves, and detect other vessels.A Reuters investigation into China’s ocean-floor mapping activities documented research and monitoring operations around Taiwan, the Philippines, Guam, and Hawaii. Although these activities can serve legitimate scientific purposes, military experts told Reuters that the resulting data could also help prepare for submarine operations.Russia remains a major undersea threatRussia presents a different but equally important challenge to the US Pacific submarine force. Cavanaugh highlighted the country’s Borei-class nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines, including newer Project 955A vessels, which provide a key component of its sea-based nuclear deterrent.He also pointed to the Yasen-class guided-missile submarines, known for their ability to carry a combination of cruise and other advanced missiles. Their quieting technology and weapons capacity make them significant threats to US naval forces.Another concern is Poseidon, Russia’s proposed nuclear-powered, nuclear-armed autonomous underwater vehicle. Also known as Status-6, the system is designed for long-range underwater operations and represents an unconventional addition to Russia’s strategic nuclear capabilities.North Korea adds another layer of uncertaintyNorth Korea’s submarine program was another concern in Cavanaugh’s assessment. The country has revealed designs for a new nuclear-powered submarine, while also claiming advances in torpedo and propulsion technology.However, the US Navy remains cautious about how much operational capability these announcements reflect. The submarine’s actual performance and the maturity of its systems have not been independently established.Taken together, developments in China, Russia, and North Korea point to an increasingly complex underwater operating environment. Cavanaugh warned that the combined growth of adversary submarine fleets could make it harder for the US Navy to maintain awareness across the vast Pacific.The challenge is not simply keeping pace with the number of submarines being built. It is maintaining the sensors, infrastructure, technology, and fleet capacity needed to detect and track them.

title: Low-cost bioprinter builds living structures more than 100 layers tall
content: Researchers at the University of Rochester and Cornell University have turned a standard 3D printer into a $450 bioprinter capable of building living structures more than 100 layers tall. The machine can also print shapes with hollow cavities, giving scientists more control over the geometry of materials that contain living cells.The researchers set out to address two problems with bioprinting: commercial machines can cost upward of $100,000, and the soft structures they produce can collapse before they set.A $450 upgrade to a standard printerA conventional 3D printer deposits molten plastic layer by layer. The team replaced the plastic filament extruder with a syringe pump that dispenses bio-ink, a mixture of living cells and a polymer solution. The ink sets into a gel after printing, holding the cells within the finished shape.The syringe can also pull back the ink. That gives the printer more control over where the material stops flowing, reducing the ooze that can blur the edges of a print.“We aim to create DIY bioprinters using inexpensive, easily obtainable parts, so that they are affordable and easy for other scientists to make in their own labs as well,” said Anne Meyer, a University of Rochester biology professor.A support gel takes prints past 100 layersEarlier DIY bioprinters could produce structures fewer than 20 layers tall. To build taller prints, the team deposited the bio-ink into a soft support gel, known as a slurry.The surrounding gel holds each layer in place while it sets, allowing the printer to keep adding material without the lower layers collapsing.The same support makes it possible to leave hollow spaces inside a print. Those cavities can expose more of the material’s surface to its surroundings. Meyer said that geometry could help embedded bacteria take up nutrients or respond to signals from their environment. It could also help substances the bacteria produce move out of the material more quickly.That control over shape could matter for applications such as treating contaminated water or breaking down plastic waste. In both cases, the choice of bacteria determines what the material can do, while its geometry influences how much of it comes into contact with its surroundings.Printed microbes survive for at least four weeksThe researchers made two versions of the support gel. One allows the finished structure to be removed easily. The other lets the team keep the print in the gel for incubation. In that version, the embedded microbes remained alive for at least four weeks. With earlier methods, printed bacteria began to die after about nine days.The longer survival period could help researchers study biofilms, the three-dimensional communities of microorganisms that grow on surfaces. The two gels give scientists options depending on what they want to examine. They could use the approach to make prints that more closely resemble medically relevant biofilms for lab studies, or produce sturdier living structures for experiments that depend on the material holding its shape.

title: China spots likely supermassive neutron star over 1.8x bigger than sun
content: Chinese astronomers examining data from the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) and the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) have found a likely supermassive neutron star accompanying a red giant, that is, neither big enough to be a black hole nor small enough to be a neutron star. This is a rarity even for astronomers and could help us understand the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes.Neutron stars are the remains of high-mass stars that have exploded. After the explosion, a star with a mass around 1.4 times that of our Sun fits into a sphere no larger than 12 miles ( 20 kilometers) across.Black holes, on the other hand, are remnants of even larger stars with mass at least five times that of the Sun to begin with. With no neutron star spotted with mass greater than 2.5 times that of the Sun, there remains a mass gap of 2.5 – 5 solar masses between them and the black holes. So, a rare spotting of an object in this mass gap opens up opportunities to understand where neutron stars give way to black holes.What did the astronomers spot? The astronomers spotted a new binary system, named J0008+0128. The binary system consists of the red giant and its companion, which was not visually confirmed. Instead, astronomers inferred its existence from its gravitational effects. This is not the first time astronomers have made such an association. However, its inferred mass, between 1.8 and 2.8 times that of the Sun, places it somewhere in the upper range of the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes, a rare and valuable find.The researchers found that the pair completes an orbit in 3.3 years, showing sufficient separation between the two. Yet the duo follows a near-circular path despite their separation. The absence of light other than that of the red giant signifies that the companion is not another regular star but a neutron star.In similar binaries, neutron stars draw material from other companions, adding to their own mass. But in this case, the neutron star is too far away to pull material from the red giant either.A neutron star or more? The astronomers conducted more than than 300,000 simulations involving binary systems to understand how such a system has been formed. Yet, none of these simulations could explain the mass and orbital properties of the system. The closest resemblance the team has for this system is Gaia NS1, a neutron star with a mass of about 1.9 suns and a two-year orbit. While J0008+0128 is a bit more extreme, it does fit all explanations. One possible explanation is that the binary system is actually a triple system with two very close small neutron stars or a neutron star and a white dwarf orbiting the red giant. Alternatively, it may have been a triple system in which the smaller bodies merged, the researchers suggest. The astronomers are confident that the formation of the system cannot be ruled out in principle and may have required a combination of extreme yet plausible parameters.The research findings were published in Science Advances.

title: China’s Arcfox launches two new EVs with 99-second battery swaps
content: Chinese automaker BAIC’s electric vehicle brand Arcfox has launched two new battery-swappable models in China, expanding the technology into a more affordable segment of the market. The Beta S3 535 Ultra+ LiDAR Swappable Edition and Beta T1 Swappable Edition both use CATL’s Chocolate battery-swapping network, with prices starting at 52,000 yuan ($7,800) under a battery-leasing arrangement.The launch builds on a partnership between BAIC and CATL to develop a shared battery-swapping ecosystem. Both cars can swap depleted battery packs in about 99 seconds, allowing drivers to resume their journeys without waiting for conventional charging.Beta S3 gets LiDAR and 535-km rangeAccording to Car News China, the Beta S3 535 Ultra+ is a front-wheel-drive electric sedan powered by a permanent-magnet synchronous motor producing 159 kW (213 hp) and 250 Nm of torque. It accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h (62 mph) in 7.1 seconds and has a top speed of 165 km/h (103 mph).Its battery delivers a claimed range of 535 km (332 miles) under China’s CLTC testing cycle. The vehicle also supports conventional fast charging.The new edition’s main technology highlight is its driver-assistance system. It combines a 192-line LiDAR sensor with Horizon Robotics’ Journey J6M computing chip to support highway and urban navigation assistance, as well as automated parking.Inside, the sedan features a 15.6-inch central touchscreen, an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8155 cockpit processor. Its starting price is 78,800 yuan ($11,800) with battery leasing.Beta T1 brings swapping to a lower priceThe smaller Beta T1 targets buyers looking for a more affordable electric car. It measures 4,337 mm (170.7 in) long, 1,860 mm (73.2 in) wide, and 1,572 mm (61.9 in) tall, with a 2,770-mm (109.1 in) wheelbase.Its electric motor produces 95 kW (127 hp), while its CATL-manufactured lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery supports the swapping system. The car has a top speed of 150 km/h (93 mph), although Arcfox has not disclosed the range of this new edition.The T1 starts at 52,000 yuan ($7,800), with a higher trim priced at 60,000 yuan ($9,000), both under battery-leasing plans.CATL expands its battery-swapping networkThe two launches are part of CATL’s wider effort to make battery swapping available across multiple vehicle brands. BAIC, CATL, and service partner CAES signed a cooperation agreement in April 2026 covering compatible vehicle development and battery-swapping infrastructure.CATL reported that its Chocolate network had more than 1,470 stations across 99 Chinese cities at the time, with a target of exceeding 3,000 stations by the end of 2026. In October, BAIC and CATL also announced a broader partnership targeting one million battery-swapping vehicles.Under battery leasing, customers purchase the car without owning its battery outright, paying a recurring fee to use a pack maintained within the swapping network. For the new Arcfox models, monthly plans start at 399 yuan ($60) for a 5,000-km (about 6,200 miles) allowance, while unlimited monthly mileage costs 599 yuan ($90).Arcfox is also offering buyers 10,000 km (about 3,100 miles) of free battery-swapping mileage through 20 vouchers. The promotion applies to Beta S3 swapping-edition purchases made by January 31, 2027, and to Beta T1 customers.The challenge for the technology will be expanding station availability. A battery exchange that takes just 99 seconds is useful only when compatible infrastructure is accessible. By bringing more affordable vehicles into the same network, BAIC and CATL are betting that shared infrastructure can make battery swapping a more practical alternative to conventional EV charging.

title: China’s Mach 3 ‘Carrier Killer’ missile with 180-mile range tested
content: The Algerian military has released footage of a test firing of what appears to be China’s export version of its YJ-12 supersonic anti-ship missile, the CM-302 (dubbed the “Carrier Killer”). Launched from a mobile defense system, the missile reportedly launched on November 10 near the city of Oran on the Mediterranean coast.The launch reportedly targeted and destroyed a target at sea as part of Algeria’s Mediterranean Falcon 2026 military exercise. By all accounts, the test was a success, with the target destroyed with what Algeria described as “great precision.”The important thing to note is that Algeria reportedly acquired the system in 2021; it hasn’t just bought it. What is new is the footage of the system in action. If the system does turn out to be the export CM-302, this would give Algeria some very serious anti-ship capabilities. It has an estimated range of 180 miles (290 km), with its missiles able to travel at between Mach 2 and 3.Low-altitude flight offers edgeEach YJ-12 missile’s payload is around 551 pounds (250 kg) of conventional explosives, and the system is designed to destroy surface vessels. Its combination of speed and low-altitude flight makes it potentially a very dangerous prospect for hostile navies.Its low-altitude flight is of particular concern, as this allows it to effectively “skim” the sea’s surface, exploiting radar’s weaknesses when it comes to scanning the horizon. Its payload is also sufficient to cause significant damage should it hit home. As for Algeria’s interest in such a weapon system, the answer appears to be area denial. The country is not in a position to field and match the naval capabilities of larger nations, especially the likes of NATO members. Systems like the CM-302, however, give Algeria the ability to avoid it altogether if it can keep ships at bay. A mobile missile battery parked somewhere on the Algerian coastline can threaten ships hundreds of miles away, forcing any potential adversary to account for that risk.This is particularly relevant in the western Mediterranean, where European naval forces regularly operate. And because the launcher is mobile, its position can change. That makes it harder to locate and neutralize than a fixed coastal missile installation. What is equally interesting here is that China appears to be more than happy to export military hardware that can challenge Western navies.Should NATO be worried?According to the reports, China has actually supplied around 27 percent of Algeria’s arms imports between 2021 and 2025. Russia is another major supplier.Beyond economics, exports of this kind not only bolster smaller nations’ defenses, but also serve as real-world demonstrations of Chinese technology of this kind. Looking at the bigger picture, this test only proves that Algeria has acquired some Chinese-built mobile anti-ship missile batteries. It doesn’t necessarily translate into a real threat for the likes of NATO members’ navies operating in the region.Having the means to hit a target, like, say, an aircraft carrier 180 miles away, is one thing. It is quite another to detect, track, and hit one at these distances without other specialist targeting hardware.

title: Inside Tesla’s 2027 plan to put its humanoid robot Optimus to work
content: At a robotics conference in Austin, Texas, in November, Tesla’s Optimus handed out snack packets to attendees. The robot could grasp a packet and hold it out for someone to take. A human was operating it remotely, according to footage from the event and reporting on the demonstration.Tesla had already begun early production of the humanoid robot in Fremont, California, by the time of the demo. The company expects its first customers to put Optimus to work on repetitive or hazardous industrial jobs.CEO Elon Musk said in October that deliveries to companies outside Tesla could begin around the end of 2027. A robot that can handle a range of chores at home is a longer-term goal.What has Optimus already done?At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Musk said some Optimus units were already doing simple tasks in Tesla’s factories. He expected them to take on more complex work by the end of 2026, still in an industrial setting. He gave few details about the jobs the robots were doing or how much human supervision they needed.The Austin demo showed how Optimus can handle a small object under remote control. Doing the same task autonomously would require the robot to work out where to grip the packet and adjust its reach as the recipient moves. It would also need to know when to let go. Those decisions matter even when the task itself looks straightforward.What jobs could Optimus do first?Musk expects industrial customers to use Optimus for jobs that people would prefer to avoid. That could include repetitive work that puts strain on workers or jobs that need to be done around the clock. Tesla has yet to specify what tasks the first customers would assign to the robot.Moving parts between workstations illustrates why a factory is a practical place to start. A part can arrive in roughly the same position each time, and the robot can repeat the same sequence. The test comes when a part is slightly out of place or slips from the robot’s grip. On a production line, the robot would need to recover and keep working without holding up the next station.Tesla plans to train Optimus by having it learn from people performing tasks and then practice those tasks in simulations and in the real world. Those practice runs would give Tesla data on how the robot moves and handles objects, which it could use to improve the software.Could Optimus do your laundry?An earlier Optimus demonstration showed the robot folding a shirt. Doing a full load of laundry would involve picking garments out of a pile, separating tangled items and working out how to fold everything from a T-shirt to a pair of jeans. A sleeve hanging over the edge of the table can change where the robot needs to grip the fabric.The hands are one of several areas Tesla says still need work. They need the dexterity to handle objects of different shapes and sizes, while the software has to adjust when something moves or a task goes wrong.The robot also needs to hold up through repeated use and operate safely around people.In October, Musk said Tesla hoped to show Optimus performing unscripted tasks within a month or two. A useful test would be to put the same snack packet in a different spot and see whether Optimus can find it, pick it up, and hand it over on its own.

title: 10 largest nuclear power plants in the US ranked by generating capacity
content: Electricity demand can swing sharply over the course of a day, but the grid needs power long after the evening rush has passed. Nuclear power helps meet that round-the-clock demand, supplying roughly one-fifth of US electricity with reactors that typically run for months between refueling outages and produce no carbon dioxide while generating power.Some nuclear stations can deliver more electricity than others simply because they have more reactors. Others can generate just as much power with fewer, larger reactors. Here are the ten largest operating nuclear power plants in the US, ranked by net summer generating capacity.1. Plant Vogtle, Georgia (4,530 MW)Wikimedia CommonsPlant Vogtle’s rise to the top was nearly four decades in the making. Its first two reactors entered commercial service in 1987 and 1989, and the site remained a two-reactor station until Unit 3 came online in 2023.Unit 4 followed in April 2024, making the eastern Georgia plant the only operating four-reactor nuclear station in the country. The two newer units account for nearly half of Vogtle’s capacity, giving it a lead of almost 600 megawatts over Palo Verde.2. Palo Verde Generating Station, Arizona (3,937 MW)Drive about 55 miles west of downtown Phoenix, and you’ll find three nuclear reactors in a place with no major body of water beside them. Palo Verde solved that siting problem by drawing on a resource the Phoenix area already produced in abundance. The resource was municipal wastewater.The station takes treated wastewater from nearby communities and processes it further for use in its cooling towers. Arizona Public Service says Palo Verde recycles more than 20 billion gallons a year, helping sustain a plant that supplies electricity across several Southwestern states.3. Browns Ferry Nuclear Plant, Alabama (3,662 MW)Browns Ferry takes its name from a ferry crossing on the Tennessee River in northern Alabama. The Tennessee Valley Authority began generating nuclear power there in 1974, and a third reactor entered commercial service in 1977.All three units are boiling-water reactors, which produce steam directly in the reactor vessel to drive their turbines. Together they put Browns Ferry more than a gigawatt ahead of fourth-place Oconee, the largest drop between any two neighbors on this list.4. Oconee Nuclear Station, South Carolina (2,600 MW)When Oconee’s first reactor entered service in July 1973, Duke Energy was building what would briefly become the world’s largest nuclear station. The three reactors still make Oconee the largest nuclear plant in Duke’s fleet and give it a narrow edge over the South Texas Project in this ranking.The plant sits on Lake Keowee, where two generations of power technology share the same waterfront. The lake supplies water for plant cooling, and the nearby Keowee hydroelectric station has historically supplied standby power as well as electricity for the grid.5. South Texas Project, Texas (2,580 MW)Wikimedia CommonsThe South Texas Project gets within 20 megawatts of Oconee with one fewer reactor. Its two pressurized-water units, which entered commercial service in 1988 and 1989, each have a net summer capacity of roughly 1,290 megawatts.The plant sits between Bay City and Palacios near the Texas Gulf Coast, but its cooling water comes from a reservoir of its own. At around 7,000 acres (about 2,830 hectares), that reservoir gives a sense of how much land the infrastructure around a two-reactor station can occupy.6. Peach Bottom Atomic Power Station, Pennsylvania (2,549 MW)Peach Bottom’s generating units are numbered 2 and 3, a reminder that the site near Delta started out with a very different reactor. Unit 1 was a high-temperature, gas-cooled demonstration reactor that shut down in 1974, the same year its two larger neighbors entered service.The operating units use boiling-water technology and together put Peach Bottom within about 31 megawatts of the South Texas Project. They also give Pennsylvania its largest nuclear station, with Susquehanna close behind.7. Susquehanna Steam Electric Station, Pennsylvania (2,494 MW)Susquehanna’s two reactors entered service in the 1980s, decades before the data center campus next door became part of the plant’s story. In June 2025, operator Talen Energy announced an expanded deal to supply electricity from the station to Amazon Web Services.The deal covers Amazon’s adjacent campus and allows deliveries to other sites in Pennsylvania. That gives the plant a role in meeting demand from cloud computing and AI at a station built more than 40 years ago.8. Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant, Texas (2,400 MW)Texas’ second entry sits inland near Glen Rose, southwest of Fort Worth. Comanche Peak’s first reactor entered commercial service in 1990, and its second followed three years later, bringing another large block of nuclear capacity onto the Texas grid.Both reactors draw cooling water from the neighboring reservoir, which absorbs heat released as steam condenses back into water. Between Comanche Peak and the South Texas Project, Texas has nearly 5,000 megawatts of nuclear generating capacity at just two sites.9. Braidwood Generating Station, Illinois (2,332 MW)Both Braidwood reactors began commercial operation in 1988, making the Will County station younger than several others on this list. Their combined capacity puts Braidwood at the top of Illinois’ nuclear fleet, ahead of Byron by roughly 32 megawatts.The plant’s cooling lake doubles as a fishing spot and waterfowl refuge. It was filled with water pumped from the Kankakee River in the early 1980s, flooding several former strip-mine pits in the process.10. McGuire Nuclear Station, North Carolina (2,316 MW)Wikimedia CommonsLake Norman was already producing electricity before McGuire’s first reactor came online. Duke created the lake in 1963 by damming the Catawba River at the Cowans Ford hydroelectric station, then built the nuclear plant on its shore near Charlotte.McGuire’s two reactors entered commercial service in 1981 and 1984, and the station uses the lake for cooling. It takes the final spot by just 5.5 megawatts over Duke’s Catawba Nuclear Station in neighboring South Carolina.ConclusionTogether, the ten largest nuclear power plants in the US have about 29 gigawatts of generating capacity. That’s nearly a third of the country’s nuclear capacity concentrated at just ten sites.Most of these plants have been generating electricity for decades. With newer reactors like those at Plant Vogtle now in service, the US relies on a mix of old and new units to keep power flowing around the clock.

title: China’s BYD targets nine-minute charging with new plug-in hybrid SUV
content: Chinese EV giant BYD is preparing to launch the Fang Cheng Bao Ti 9, a full-size six-seat plug-in hybrid SUV built around a combination of high-output electric motors, a 66.48 kWh Blade Battery, and an unusually fast charging system. The company said its flash-charging technology can take the battery from 10 percent to 97 percent in nine minutes, potentially making charging speed one of the model’s main selling points.The Ti 9 will officially launch in China on November 19, ahead of its public appearance at the 2026 Guangzhou Auto Show. Fang Cheng Bao general manager Xiong Tianbo said earlier that display vehicles had reached 21 dealerships across 12 cities, with deliveries underway in another 20 cities.The launch follows the opening of reservations earlier in November. A Ti 9 also rolled off BYD’s Xi’an production line that day as the company’s 19 millionth new energy vehicle, marking a production milestone for the Chinese automaker.Dual electric motors deliver 536 hpThe Ti 9 uses BYD’s sixth-generation DM-i plug-in hybrid system, pairing a 1.5-liter turbocharged gasoline engine with two permanent magnet synchronous electric motors.The combustion engine produces 154 hp, while each electric motor is rated at 268 hp. Together, the motors provide a combined peak electric output of 536 hp. According to reports, the configuration gives the SUV substantial electric propulsion capacity while retaining a gasoline engine for longer journeys.Energy comes from a 66.48 kWh second-generation lithium iron phosphate Blade Battery. BYD claims an all-electric driving range of 193 miles under the Worldwide harmonized Light vehicles Test Cycle (WLTC). With a full battery and fuel tank, the Ti 9 has a claimed combined range of 1,013 miles under China’s CLTC testing standard. The estimated equivalent under the WLTP cycle is about 808 to 861 miles, though real-world range depends on driving conditions and vehicle configuration.When the battery is depleted, fuel consumption is rated at 36.8 mpg under WLTC testing. These figures position the Ti 9 as a large hybrid SUV designed to combine substantial electric driving capability with the flexibility of a conventional fuel-powered vehicle.Nine minutes flash chargingThe most notable technology claim for the Ti 9 model is the flash-charging system. BYD claims the system can charge the battery from 10 percent to 70 percent in five minutes and reach 97 percent in nine minutes.The company also claims that the system can charge the battery from 20 percent to 97 percent in 12 minutes at temperatures as low as minus 22 degrees Fahrenheit. That cold-weather figure is particularly relevant because low temperatures can reduce battery charging performance and increase charging times.The 66.48 kWh Blade Battery uses lithium iron phosphate chemistry, which BYD has developed across its electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle lineup. The second-generation battery is central to the Ti 9’s claimed electric range and rapid-charging capability.However, BYD has not disclosed the peak charging power, the precise charging infrastructure required to achieve the advertised times, or the conditions under which the figures were recorded. Those details will be important for assessing how readily the technology can be used outside controlled testing conditions.

title: China holds 80% of underwater data center patents in past 20 years
content: A new study has found that China owns around 80 percent of all global underwater data center patents. That’s not to say China owns much of the technology used in these setups, but it does reveal how active it has been in patenting in this field.The study’s findings come from two Chinese researchers analyzing 168 patents filed between 2006 and 2026. It appears to show that technological focus has shifted quite dramatically over this time.Before about 2014, patents were dominated by American, Norwegian, and Canadian researchers exploring underwater enclosures and pressure protection. Between about 2015 and 2020, attention turned to cooling, electrical supply, and long-term reliability. From 2021, Chinese researchers became the dominant source for patents, particularly focusing on modular construction and maintenance. They also found that China holds the lion’s share, with South Korea owning around 17, and the rest split between the US and Europe.China appears to hold the most patentsChinese patents in particular focus on the actual construction, installation, connections, and maintenance of them at scale. This appears to show that China is shifting focus to the more practical elements rather than proving experimental technology. All very interesting, but why all the interest? Well, data centers generate an enormous amount of heat when in operation. This comes from the conversion of electricity into heat by the vast number of computer processors.Typically, this is handled by using a combination of fans, chillers, cooling towers, and liquid-cooling systems to manage temperatures. That is costly in terms of hardware and additional electricity costs.If the centers could be placed underwater, they could take advantage of the ocean’s near-limitless supply of very cold seawater. Obviously, you can’t just submerge the hardware directly into the ocean, so they need to be placed inside sealed, pressure-resistant containers first.These are then lowered and secured to the seabed, and connections are made to the shore for power and data cables. Once there, the heat from the servers can be transferred to the cold ocean water using special internal cooling systems. To this end, the seawater acts as a massive heat sink, potentially eliminating much of the mechanical cooling equipment needed on land. This doesn’t make the computers themselves consume less electricity, but it can reduce the energy spent keeping them cool.China is taking the lead in underwater data centersAnd it is not just a theoretical technology either. Famously, Microsoft deployed one, called Project Natick, off the coast of Scotland in 2018. The project ran for around two years, and results were very encouraging.According to Microsoft, the underwater data center had just one-eighth of the failure rate of similar land-based setups. Yet despite this, Microsoft chose not to commercialize the technology, and confirmed in 2024 that the project had been discontinued.So, is the 80 percent figure something other nations should sit up and take notice of? Yes, and no. It is clear China has established some kind of lead here in terms of patents, but the engineering challenges of actually deploying them are enormous. The shift in focus to modularity likely reflects China’s ambitions to scale the technology commercially. But it is important to note that patents tend to be territorial in nature. Holding a large share of patents in a particular field doesn’t automatically give a country control of the technology worldwide.

title: Miniature solar cells offer wireless control of living cell alignment
content: Researchers at Pennsylvania State University (Penn State) have developed a way to control the alignment of living cells using miniature solar cells, potentially offering a wireless alternative to bulky electrical systems used in tissue engineering.The approach uses tiny photovoltaic cells patterned across silicon chips to convert light into local electrical fields that influence how cells orient themselves. By changing the size and arrangement of these microscopic solar cells, researchers can guide groups of cells into specific patterns without connecting electrodes directly to them.The technique could eventually help scientists organize cells more precisely when developing biological tissues through 3D bioprinting.Miniature solar cells guide alignmentBioprinting uses living cells and biological materials, known as bioink, to build tissues layer by layer. Keeping these cells organized is important because their alignment can influence how tissues develop and function.Researchers have traditionally used electrical stimulation to influence cell orientation. However, these systems often rely on bulky equipment, wired electrodes, and invasive connections that make precise control more difficult.To address this, the Penn State team developed patterned arrays of silicon photovoltaic microcells. These tiny devices capture light and convert it into electrical signals, generating local fields that influence cellular behavior.In a study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the researchers tested two approaches. They changed the diameter of individual photovoltaic cells, ranging from 80 to 800 micrometers, and experimented with different arrangements while keeping the cell size constant.The team placed commercially sourced human lung and skin fibroblasts on the silicon chips. Fibroblasts are connective-tissue cells that help produce and maintain the structural framework surrounding tissues.The samples were exposed to different light intensities over seven days. The researchers then compared their alignment with cells grown on chips that received no illumination.Light patterns influence growthThe results showed that fibroblasts grown without illumination displayed largely random alignment. Cells exposed to light, however, arranged themselves according to the patterns of the photovoltaic arrays.The researchers also found that changing the illumination intensity influenced the electrical response of the solar cells, providing another way to regulate cellular alignment.By adjusting the size, spacing and arrangement of the photovoltaic microcells, the team could modify the electrical fields generated across the chip.The approach does not provide complete control over cell organization, as interactions between neighboring cells still influence their movement and orientation. However, it demonstrates how light-powered electrical stimulation can guide groups of living cells without wired electrodes.The researchers now plan to test the technique on more sensitive cell types, including cardiac and muscle cells, to investigate whether electrical stimulation can also influence their functions.They also want to move beyond flat surfaces and explore three-dimensional environments. This could allow photovoltaic arrays to generate electrical fields in different directions, offering greater control over how cells organize themselves within developing tissues.The findings could eventually support more precise tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, although further work is needed before the approach can be applied to functional 3D-printed tissues.

title: China debuts 4,000-kilowatt rescue ship with 360-degree propulsion
content: China has completed its first batch of five domestically designed medium-sized maritime rescue vessels, strengthening its ability to respond to emergencies along its coastline. The final vessel, Donghai Jiu 152, officially joined the Ministry of Transport’s Donghai Rescue Bureau on November 13, 2026. The 4,000-kilowatt vessel brings several specialized capabilities to China’s eastern coastal waters. Its propulsion and positioning systems allow crews to operate in challenging maritime conditions. The ship can also support rescue missions involving large numbers of survivors.The delivery marks the end of a nearly seven-year procurement program. China delivered the first vessel, Donghai Jiu 151, in December 2019.Designed for coastal emergenciesMeasuring 69.5 meters (228 feet) long and 14.6 meters (48 feet) wide, Donghai Jiu 152 targets rescue operations across China’s eastern waters. Its hull and onboard systems accommodate demanding conditions along exposed coastlines.The vessel can withstand strong winds and carries an external firefighting system. It also has enough capacity to accommodate up to 100 rescued people. That capacity gives rescue crews additional flexibility during large-scale maritime emergencies.Its equipment also supports operations beyond conventional search and rescue missions. An advanced azimuthing electric propulsion system provides precise maneuverability. This setup helps the vessel navigate confined waters and maintain control during demanding operations.A Class 2 dynamic positioning system (DP-2) further expands its operational capabilities. The system helps the ship maintain a designated position without relying entirely on conventional anchoring. Such technology proves particularly useful when crews conduct operations near islands, reefs, or other difficult coastal terrain.Electric propulsion improves controlDynamic positioning plays an important role in modern offshore and maritime operations. DP-2 systems use computerized controls to coordinate propulsion and maintain a vessel’s position. They can compensate for external forces such as wind, waves, and currents.Donghai Jiu 152 also carries a three-point anchoring arrangement. Captain He Feng said the system helps the vessel remain stable in shallow water. It can maintain that position under Sea State 3 conditions, according to CCTV News.That capability supports diving operations, which require a relatively stable working platform. Maintaining position in shallow water can prove difficult when currents and changing weather affect a vessel. The additional anchoring arrangement gives the crew another way to manage those conditions.Seven-year construction programChina began receiving the first vessel in this series in December 2019. The Donghai Rescue Bureau took delivery of Donghai Jiu 151 on December 25 that year. The vessel established the foundation for four subsequent ships.In December 2022, China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC) signed contracts for four additional vessels. The shipbuilder developed the new designs using Donghai Jiu 151 as their foundation.The subsequent vessels also incorporated upgrades to digital systems and network connectivity. These improvements aim to support better coordination during maritime rescue operations.Completing the five-vessel program gives China’s rescue authorities additional coverage across nearshore waters. The broader emergency response network combines vessels of different sizes with maritime, land, and aerial resources. Together, these assets help authorities coordinate operations across varying distances and rescue scenarios.The new fleet also addresses a gap in China’s nearshore emergency response capabilities. Its medium-sized vessels can handle missions that may demand more capacity than smaller rescue boats provide. Their specialized equipment also allows crews to tackle operations in challenging coastal environments.

title: Google's Antigravity agents formalise major mathematical proofs
content: Google has expanded its Antigravity multi-agent system, using teams of specialized agents powered by its Gemini models to tackle longstanding mathematical problems, verify complex proofs and optimize software systems.The company said its Teamwork framework has helped researchers formalize landmark mathematical results, identify molecular structures and develop faster software implementations. The work combines human expertise with multiple agents that independently explore solutions, test approaches and verify results using computational tools.Among the most notable results is the formalization of the Weil conjectures, a landmark set of mathematical results concerning the number of solutions to polynomial equations over finite fields. Google’s Teamwork-LEAP system produced approximately 1.8 million lines of Lean code across 28,800 subagent invocations to formalize the results, originally proved by mathematician Pierre Deligne in 1974.Google said the system also reproduced a formalization of a recent proof concerning finite-time blowup in the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations, a problem connected to one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems. The question of whether smooth solutions to these equations can develop singularities in finite time has remained open for about 90 years.Agents verify complex proofsThe system also helped researchers address the Courtade–Kumar conjecture, an information theory problem first proposed in 2013. Researchers from Google and academic institutions used the framework to develop a proof in full generality, with Gemini models helping derive analytical bounds and generate computer-checkable certificates.The researchers formalized the proof in Lean 4, a programming language and proof assistant that lets a computer check mathematical arguments.Google’s approach relies on multiple agents working in parallel, with separate systems assigned to challenge and verify proposed solutions. This is intended to reduce errors that can emerge when a single model generates a long chain of reasoning.Each specialized agent receives only the files and tools required for its task. Independent critics and auditors then examine the results without relying on the original agent’s reasoning.Beyond mathematics, Google applied the approach to molecular chemistry. A team of 30 specialized agents working with a physics-informed simulator identified molecular structures from nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data with 95% top-one accuracy and 100% top-three accuracy on complex benchmark molecules.Software gains from teamworkThe framework also delivered results in systems engineering. Google said its agents rewrote the company’s libgav1 AV1 video decoder from C++ into approximately 170,000 lines of Rust code, achieving exact output parity across a broad testing suite.The initial rewrite ran about four times slower than the original implementation. After the agents were given access to profiling tools and tasked with improving performance, the Rust version became 20% to 30% faster than the original C++ implementation on both x86_64 and ARM processors.In another project, a two-week campaign rewrote the remaining C++ code in the Zircon microkernel into approximately 800,000 lines of memory-safe Rust, passing kernel unit tests and booting on ARM64 hardware.Google also reported improvements in its internal infrastructure. Its agentic scheduling workflow reduced TPU workload preemption by 24% on some hardware types while maintaining service-level objectives and cluster utilization.The company is making Teamwork and its iterative coding workflow, /boost, available through Antigravity. Google also opened applications for 10,000 academic researchers to receive six months of free access to its highest usage tier.The company said additional specialized workflows, including formal proof tools, will be made available in the future.

title: Elon Musk joins petition to bring Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO
content: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has sparked an unexpected show of support from employees, political figures and technology executives. Elon Musk has joined the campaign to restore Huang to the company’s top position, revealing Friday that he will be signing a petition supporting his return. The former CEO resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman alleged to have connections to Chinese intelligence.Support for the former Nvidia chief has also emerged from within the chipmaker. Internal employee feedback reportedly shows considerable opposition to losing the executive who helped build Nvidia into one of the world’s most influential technology companies.Musk rallies behind HuangMusk announced his endorsement in a post on X, adding his name to the growing list of prominent figures backing Huang. The Tesla and SpaceX chief had previously defended the executive and expressed interest in bringing him aboard his own companies. He described the prospect of working with Huang as an honor.A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 13, 2026An internal post asking Nvidia’s board to consider employee sentiment has attracted more than 1,600 comments, according to WIRED. A longtime engineer submitted the suggestion before Huang’s resignation. Most responses reportedly favored bringing him back.One anonymous employee called for Huang’s reinstatement, arguing that the company needed its longtime leader. Another suggested that the executive deserved a second chance. An employee also sent a companywide email expressing continued support for Huang.The internal response has coincided with several public campaigns. A Change.org petition titled “Bring Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO” appeared on November 12. Its creator, Mohamed Adany, identifies himself as an Nvidia shareholder. The campaign had collected 170 verified signatures by Friday evening.A separate letter circulating on social media allegedly represents hundreds of Nvidia employees demanding Huang’s return. It reportedly threatens employee departures to join a SpaceX chip project. However, the document’s authenticity remains unverified.Its wording also closely resembles a 2023 employee letter supporting Sam Altman during his removal from OpenAI. That similarity raises questions about the document’s origins.Trump weighs in on Huang’s exitPresident Donald Trump has also defended Huang, praising his leadership during an interview with sports broadcaster Stephen A. Smith. He credited the executive with Nvidia’s extraordinary success and described him as an exceptionally talented business leader.Trump also revealed that he spoke with Huang on Wednesday, shortly before the resignation. According to the president, their conversation focused heavily on the personal consequences of the controversy. Huang reportedly expressed regret about the damage the situation had caused his wife and family.When Smith asked whether Huang should have resigned, Trump pointed to the unresolved allegations involving Alice Huang. He said the key question was whether she actually worked as a Chinese spy.Trump suggested that Huang’s departure made sense if investigators established those allegations as true. However, he indicated that the circumstances could warrant a different assessment if she had no intelligence connections.Despite the controversy, Trump expressed confidence that Huang would recover professionally. He also maintained a favorable personal impression of the former Nvidia chief.
